#6645. Everything Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams Have Said About Their Friendship

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

HBO Max and Crave’s Heated Rivalry has quickly become one of the most-discussed series of the year, catapulting its stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams into the celebrity stratosphere. The two actors portray hockey players Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie), who have a secret love affair spanning almost a decade. The series is known for its spicy intimate scenes as well as its beautiful depiction of romantic yearning.

Storrie and Williams have been open in interviews about their experience creating the show, along with their offscreen relationship as they navigate sudden fame together.

“Hudson is my best friend, and I literally can’t fathom doing this without him,” Storrie told W magazine in December 2025. “We were both in similar places in life before this. We quit our jobs within a day of each other. We booked this and flew out the same day. Now it’s turning into two people who are being seen internationally for the first time. This has been the highlight of my life, and meeting Hudson makes that 10 times sweeter.”

Here, everything the two actors have shared about their friendship.

Fans of the show tend to “ship” Williams and Storrie, hoping they end up dating in real life. Storrie addressed this head-on in an interview with Vulture, saying things are strictly platonic.

When asked about the intimate scenes they shot in the show, Storrie said, “For me, it doesn’t feel spicy at all—like, that’s me and my best friend. This is the first time in my life I’m having this many eyes on me. They’ve seen me naked, they’ve seen me kiss, they’ve seen me be in love with a man on-screen—it’s only normal for people to try to transfer that over to mine and Hudson’s real life.” He explained that he intends to keep his private life private, adding, “I feel honored to be able to bring someone to life that so many people feel seen, understood, and represented by, and I think that transcends whoever I’m sleeping with in my real life.”

Williams expressed a similar sentiment to Deadline, saying, “I want queer people telling queer stories, but also, there’s the element of Connor and I—we’re best friends, and we love expressing that physically. You see people who infer or assume, and you kind of have to let that go. But then again, I never wanna stop expressing the love I have for Connor physically, and I’m never really going to, and I think multiple things can be true at once.”

In November 2026, Williams’s interview on The Assembly aired. One of the audience members there asked Williams if he ever had romantic feelings for Storrie. “No,” he replied. “Quickly, me and Connor realized we were, like, platonic soulmates, just completely in love with each other. I think that’s what made our friendship so stable and beautiful, is that we realized we could be completely ourselves, be completely guard down. So, I think the thing that made our relationship as rich as it was is, like, me and that man could cuddle for 10 hours, and it just mean cuddling, just mean we just love each other dearly, but don’t wanna beep each other’s bop.”

He then added playfully, “Who doesn’t want Connor Storrie in their shower? You know, someone needs to get my back. I wish Connor was just with me every day. I’m like, ‘Hey, I have a loofah but I can’t reach [my back].’ If I had Connor with me every day, he could just come in there.”

Sophie Nélisse, who plays Heated Rivalry’s Rose Landry, interviewed Williams for Wonderland magazine in January 2026 and asked him how he and Storrie balance promoting the show with forging their own identities. Williams admitted that they purposely go to different events, in part to keep their friendship more private and their brands separate.

“It’s been really nice, because Connor and I are aligned,” Williams began. “We want to be different artists. We don’t want to be the Olsen twins. We want to be Connor and Hudson, with different filmographies and different deals. As much as we love each other, our friendship doesn’t need to be public. Jacob [Tierney] has that quote: ‘Shane and Ilya are for the public. Connor and Hudson are for themselves.’ And that’s how we feel. People want to see us front row together all the time, but we actively avoid that, because it starts to feel like branding. If you’re always seen together, you become attached at the hip. I FaceTime him whenever I’m free. But if we’re offered the same fashion shows, we’re like, ‘Which one are you going to? Okay, I’ll go to a different one.’ We’re stubborn, selfish artists who want to be our own people. We’re like, ‘I love you. I don’t want to do everything with you.’”

Both Williams and Storrie got into great shape for the show. In a profile with GQ in December 2025, Williams talked about meeting his co-star and being intimidated by his build.

“Connor pushed himself up onto the island in the kitchen,” Williams said. “I remember seeing his arms. They were the size of my legs. I was like, Holy fuck.”

“It’s not true,” Storrie responded. “Because you have crazy legs.”

The show’s creator, Jacob Tierney, also commented on their affection for one another in the piece, saying, “They’re living through a thing right now that is bananas—absolutely fucking bananas—and they’re handling it with grace, with humor, with generosity. They adore each other, which is like, thank fucking God.”

While discussing his own workout routine with Men’s Health in January, Williams had a playful quip about Storrie’s physique: “I’m okay talking about my butt, but poor Connor Storrie—who has the fattest butt I’ve ever seen on a man—I’m sure just wants to stop talking about his beautiful cheeks.”

In a December interview with Entertainment Weekly, the friends discussed a viral video from the Heated Rivalry wrap party where they are rolling around on the floor together.

“Very plainly spoken, me and Hudson are freaks,” Storrie explained. “We’re clowns. We just love to riff and have fun and go crazy, and those were two situations where we were caught off guard doing our thing. The wrap party, that was all improvised. I think we were just putting on a show.”

Williams added, “Also, there might be something else, I think, with—we’re both very physical actors, and movement is a huge part of it.”

During his Vulture interview, Storrie spoke about moving into an apartment next to Williams’s while filming in Toronto.

“We would literally just go to set, go home, cook, work out together, and geek out over how excited we were to finally be working on this level,” he said. “If we were any less close, we probably would’ve gotten annoyed with each other really quick.”

The American actor told Vulture that they leaned into their chemistry while promoting Heated Rivalry’s first season. “If Hudson says something jokingly, like, ‘Spit in my mouth,’ I think that gives everyone else the go-ahead to get in on that too,” he said. “People are ruthless talking about our holes and our butts.”

During his discussion with Interview, Storrie added that spending time with Williams has helped ground them both during their press tour. “Hudson’s been in town, so we’ll have some quality time and come back down to ground zero,” he said. “It’s funny, because all the press and stuff is getting easier and easier and easier. You would think you would get burnt out and exhausted. Even though it’s only been three weeks of doing press for this, I’m clicking into an interesting sort of confidence and appreciation for all of this.”

Williams, meanwhile, credited Storrie for helping him keep the press tour fun during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “I have one of my best friends for life right beside me through it all, which is already a luxury that a lot of actors don’t get,” he said. “I’m sure I would’ve probably had a smaller appetite for the amount of stuff we’re doing if I didn’t have him through this. I’m an omnivert, leaning more to an extrovert, but I still get—I have ADHD, I’m unmedicated, currently, for the last while, so my social battery can just tap [out] pretty quick. At the end of the day, I’m pretty forgiving with myself if I’m talking with a reporter in a polite, more boring way. Then when I’ve had coffee, and I’ve had a nap, I let myself be chaotic. I let myself off the leash. I try to say, whatever mood I’m in, just be Canadian, don’t be mean. Whatever they get, they get.”

Timid magazine asked Williams how Storrie’s acting has helped him be a better performer. Williams responded, “He’s so incredibly present and so incredibly truthful. As an actor, it’s so much easier to think of what you should be doing or what you think would be an entertaining version of this or the most dramatic version or make sure you’re hitting these lines properly or doing the scene properly or the director wants this and the script says this. But just to actually listen to the person and let what they’re saying affect you—Connor is so good at that. There’s so many moments where I am saying something and the script says he does this, and he does something so unexpectedly emotional or so unexpectedly vulnerable that even if I’m very robotic and going through a scene, he can crack me and change my trajectory in the scene. He’s a huge resource in affecting me and that makes my job way easier because I don’t have to. He makes me be present. He’s so good at that. That’s his superpower.”

Storrie, meanwhile, credited Williams for helping him understand Ilya so quickly in his Interview story. “I feel like I got the character pretty instantly,” he began. “I believed in his circumstances without almost any effort, and I just trusted Hudson so much. It’s so easy to act when you know where you’re coming from and you believe the person opposite you. I mean, I’m so gooey. I’m such a romantic. So any of the really heightened emotional moments—their love or confession or an outbreak or a fight—those are the moments that I really enjoy as an actor.”

Williams listed out all the nicknames he and Storrie have for each other during his Timid magazine interview. “He calls me Huddy, Papi, Bubba, Baby,” he said. “I call him Pookie. I used to call him Pookie a lot. Papi. Oh, Con Con. I call him that both in text form and verbally. But yeah, a lot of nicknames.”

GQ revealed that when the series wrapped, they got matching tattoos that read “SEX SELLS.”

The Canadian star revealed that he stayed at Storrie’s Los Angeles apartment when he came to the U.S. to do some press. “We were like, ‘Oh, my God, if people saw us just getting ready in the morning, giving each other big spooning hugs, just to say we’re proud of each other,’ people would be going crazy,” he told Variety. “If only one fan had access, God forbid. But yeah, we just love each other very dearly.”

The outlet asked him what creating Heated Rivalry taught him. Williams responded, “I think I had my own biases, maybe that would be too strong of a word, but my own discomfort if I expressed myself fully, physically and affectionately, both with women and men. It would feel inappropriate. I realized if you really do love someone—platonically or not—I’m such a tactile, sensory person. There are so many taboos. It’s much harder on men. I had to let that go, and I got to learn how freeing that is. That also went hand-in-hand with being myself, truly as an artist. Connor was also a great person to have at my side. I think we both opened each other up to just be freer, more fully expressive.”

During Williams’s January 2026 appearance on Andy Cohen Live, he revealed that Storrie is an “awful texter,” but they largely keep in touch with frequent video calls. “We’ll Facetime each other or call each other randomly, very consistently,” he told the host. “That has sort of been my stability, especially through this. Just having my best friend who is in the same position I am.”

In a November 2025 interview with The Permanent Rain Press, Williams said he would pitch Storrie as “a beautiful little, sensitive little radical, artist boy. Who should be treated with the utmost care and hugs and friendliness because he can’t handle anything else. And that’s perfect. And that’s the way he should be treated.”

He added, “And anyone who doesn’t treat him that way should die.”

In May 2026, Williams and Storrie made their Met Gala debut. They took a bathroom selfie together, which Williams later posted to his Threads account.

The pair’s appearance at the Met Gala excited fans, with one user taking a solo shot of Williams and posting it alongside lyrics from Rihanna’s breakup song, “Woo.” (Williams has a longtime girlfriend, Katelyn Larson.) The post has since been taken down, but Williams responded and wrote, “Rpfing [real person fan fiction] gotta stop y’all.”

During his November interview on Vogue’s The Run-Through podcast, Storrie revealed that he and Williams were living together while shooting season 2 of Heated Rivalry.

“Right now we’re filming [the next season of Heated Rivalry], so I literally live with him, which is amazing,” he said. “We were at this hotel, which was a brilliant hotel, but I just….I needed a washing machine. I needed a kitchen.”

Storrie also discussed how their red carpet looks sometimes seem coordinated without any advance planning, pointing to their similar outfits at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party.

“We’ve had a few moments where it just matched. But that’s just very telling of Hudson and I in general. We are very cut from the same cloth. We have a soul tie thing. So there’s a lot of synchronicity. But no, we don’t coordinate before at all,” he said.

He also expressed admiration for Williams’s personal style, particularly his approach to streetwear and tailoring.

“Hudson is really cool. You know what I mean? Hudson has this sort of, there’s something kind of like street style or edgy about what he does,” Storrie explained. “And like when he dresses up, when he does like fine suits and tailoring, it’s a little bit different. And I always kind of envy that, like him being able to wear really cool stuff, because it doesn’t really work the same on me. But I like my thing too.”

#6644. Gigi Hadid Takes a Cozy Winter Walk in a Structured Topcoat and Slouchy Boots

It’s that time of the year again. Heading into the holiday season, Gigi Hadid broke out her cozy winter layers—bundling up in browns for a late-November walk in New York City.

For the outing, the model played with contrasts, pairing a structured topcoat with slouchy boots. The outerwear, courtesy of Helsa, was crafted from deep-chocolate wool with sharp, sculpted shoulder pads and wide peak lapels that added a distinctly formal feel to the piece.

The width of the top half was only exaggerated further by a tapered waist, which was tailored with darting for a snug fit. At the hips, two flap pockets were stitched into the fabric.

Underneath, Hadid wore a baby-blue crewneck knit with rolled edges, and a pair of black sweatpants that were mostly hidden by her coat. Her shoes, the aforementioned slouchy pair, were Miu Miu’s take on workwear boots, with worn-in leather and a relaxed (though sturdy) construction.

For an extra bit of warmth, she added a latte-brown brushed cashmere beanie from her Guest in Residence label. The piece was reversible, and at one point during the day, she turned it inside out to reveal a striped pattern in shades of cream, light blue, and brown.

On her ring finger, Hadid wore her diamond-dotted Boucheron wedding band. The model was first seen wearing the ring in early August, during a trip to Paris with partner Bradley Cooper. He wore a similar band from the same jeweler, and both were reportedly purchased as promise rings, representing the couple’s commitment to one another.

#6643. Forget the Film Stars—2026 Belonged to the Best-Dressed Directors

While scrolling through my Instagram feed last week, I came across a pair of T-shirts made by Sofia Coppola for Mack Books. To celebrate the release of her mother Eleanor’s documentary, Making Marie Antoinette—a portrait compiled from archival footage shot during the making of Coppola’s 2006 cult classic—as well as the original film’s 20th anniversary, Coppola has released a limited-edition capsule collection printed with on-set photography by Andrew Durham. Naturally, I had a T-shirt in my basket faster than you could say “Let them eat cake.” (In case you were wondering, I went for the one with Kirsten Dunst looking wistfully out from a rococo horse-drawn carriage, a camera rig looming in the foreground.)

But it also got me thinking, not for the first time, about film directors and fashion. There’s a reason why the behind-the-scenes photos from that movie—Dunst and Jason Schwartzman in powdered wigs and full Versailles regalia listening to their iPods, Coppola crouched behind a monitor in a button-down and jeans; you know the ones—have remained such an enduring touchstone within the online cultural consciousness, from Tumblr to TikTok. There’s something both fascinating and lightly absurd about the friction between the practical, gorpy clothing worn by most on a film set and the breathtaking opulence of the period costuming. And in Making Marie Antoinette, Coppola’s casual but stylish on-set wardrobe of well-cut mid-aughts basics is, counterintuitively, almost as captivating as Milena Canonero’s glorious 18th-century costume confections. Which I guess is partly why Coppola made those T-shirts.

But it’s also partly why the best directors—those who spend their lives building worlds and poring over the details of what their character might say, do, and, most importantly for our purposes, wear—have become as compelling to watch on the red carpet as the contract-bound movie stars they direct. (It’s little wonder that some of history’s greatest filmmakers were also some of history’s most stylish, possessing an innate understanding of the storytelling power of clothes: Agnès Varda, David Lynch, Wong Kar-wai, the list goes on.)

Which brings me to the 2026 awards trail—and the 2027 awards trail, which is now kicking into gear—where the sartorial approaches have been refreshingly eclectic. While promoting Sinners, Ryan Coogler’s killer red carpet looks included a three-piece Thom Browne suit with a diamond brooch at the Golden Globes, a slouchy Fear of God suit at the SAG Awards, and a sharp Louis Vuitton tux at the Oscars.

Ryan Coogler (with his wife, Zinzi) in Thom Browne at the Golden Globes.

For Chloé Zhao—who, not coincidentally, earned a spot on this year’s Vogue best dressed list—campaigning for Hamnet appeared to involve taking cues from the world of her film. (Turns out directors can do method dressing too.) Working with Gabriela Hearst, she wore a gold gown with a Tudor-inflected Basque waist at the BAFTAs, while at the Academy Awards, she wore a headline-grabbing gown inspired by Victorian mourning dress—complete with draped bell sleeves, Bulgari diamonds, and a sheer black veil—that she described as “the alchemical image of the crow.” Try getting that level of commitment from a leading man in a black tux and a brand-deal watch.

Chloé Zhao in Gabriela Hearst at the BAFTAs.

Thankfully, this year, there’s a new crop of fashion-fluent directors ready to take up the mantle. Just take Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known collectively as Los Javis, who have happily matched the maximalist, operatic sweep of their Lorca-inspired epic La Bola Negra with their steady stream of playful tailoring—coordinating Loewe suits at the Biarritz Film Festival, say, or oversized shirting and denim to the Chanel show over the summer—proving their flair for the visual extends well beyond the silver screen.

Los Javis—or Javi Ambrossi and Javi Calvo—at the GQ Men of the Year Awards in Madrid.

Ambrossi and Calvo in Chanel at the brand’s haute couture fall 2026 show.

Meanwhile, Olivia Wilde has been delivering some of the year’s sharpest high-low looks while promoting The Invite—everything from a custom Saint Laurent dress with an ab-baring cutout at the Los Angeles premiere, to a boxy black vintage tee and double-pleated pants from The Row for a SAG-AFTRA event. “I really love not having to dress up in the same way as I have as an actress,” she told Chloe Malle on the Vogue podcast earlier this year. “I do feel like after decades of tarting myself up for press tours, I am so relieved to be like, ‘You know what? They wear T-shirts. I’m gonna wear a fucking T-shirt.’” (Granted, wearing a T-shirt hits a little differently when it’s tucked into pants that cost roughly the same as a secondhand Honda Civic, but the point stands.)

Olivia Wilde in Saint Laurent at The Invite’s Los Angeles premiere.

Wilde in a vintage x Karla tee and The Row pants at a SAG-AFTRA Foundation event.

Then, there’s Greta Gerwig, who’s gearing up for the February release of her rock-opera-inspired Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew, whose looks this year—Bottega Veneta, Stella McCartney, Diotima by Rachel Scott—hint at a bold (and largely female-designed) press tour wardrobe to come.

Greta Gerwig in Bottega Veneta at the PGA Awards.

Gerwig in Ashlyn at the opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art.

And finally, for a new vanguard of filmmakers, the press tour has become a place to subvert the traditional codes of men’s tailoring. On that front, there’s Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman and the Bottega Veneta suit he wore for the Los Angeles premiere, with its oversized powder-pink collar peeking over the top of the lapels, or the Tom Ford by Haider Ackermann jacket for the New York premiere that featured a silk floral boutonnière with a flowing ribbon. Or Jane Schoenbrun, who debuted their queer slasher, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, in Cannes with a series of offbeat looks that included a particularly delightful puffball skirt suit with powder-blue tights and Mary Janes.

Jordan Firstman in Tom Ford by Haider Ackermann at the New York premiere of Club Kid.

Jane Schoenbrun at the Cannes premiere of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.

It helps, of course, that in 2026, the lines between luxury fashion houses and cinema have all but dissolved. Fashion is no longer just dressing actors and directors for the premiere, or awards show; it’s actively financing, producing, and inserting itself into their work. In September, Dior announced a two-year creative partnership with A24 before doubling down just this week with a new Sundance Institute fellowship supporting women filmmakers. The Anthony Vaccarello–founded Saint Laurent Productions has cemented itself as a Cannes and awards-season powerhouse, backing auteurs such as Jim Jarmusch and Claire Denis. And some designers are stepping into the film set trenches, too—most notably Jonathan Anderson, who followed up his work on Challengers and Queer by designing the costumes for Guadagnino’s hotly anticipated Silicon Valley satire Artificial.

Clothes maketh the man. All of these directors know that clothes maketh the character. So let’s hope that, this awards season, clothes continue to maketh the filmmaker, too—and if they ever run out of ideas, I’ve got a Marie Antoinette T-shirt they’re welcome to borrow.

#6642. A Rare Alexander McQueen Gem Is Coming to Auction

The iconic Alexander McQueen “Plato’s Atlantis” dress is headlining Christie’s December Luxury Week.

Few remnants of fashion history manage to stir up emotions and draw headlines quite like pieces from Alexander McQueen’s revered runways. Rare, technical, and sensorial, these are certainly not your average, everyday pieces of clothing. McQueen runway pieces are often flexed at the world’s top fashion exhibitions at museums around the world. That’s just one of the reasons why the multicolor silk minidress from Alexander McQueen spring/summer 2010 “Plato’s Atlantis” is the star of Christie’s December Luxury Week, where the runway gem will be hitting the auction block with a $150,000 to $300,000 estimate. The sale runs online from November 25 to December 10, 2026.

“Based on what we know about McQueen’s distribution at the time and the types of garments that went into production after a runway show, we estimate there were probably only fewer than two dozen examples of this exact dress produced,” Max Brownawell, head of handbags at Christie’s, tells ELLE. “Then on top of that, the importance of ‘Plato’s Atlantis,’ as McQueen’s final fully realized collection, really can’t be understated. He himself said that his previous collection was his final as a young man. And so this was his most mature, fully fledged collection that he’d ever produced.”

The dress was the fourth look in the runway collection, styled with the iconic Armadillo boots. Designed with a futuristic sculpted drape, covered in prints from the natural world (think: a collage of abstracted imagery pulled from butterfly wings, snakeskin, and insects), the silhouette is a favorite of fashion fans and archivists. Brownawell shares that the piece still has the tag attached and has likely never been worn. The ensemble may very well exceed the estimate: for reference, a “Plato’s Atlantis” look complete with those aforementioned boots sold for $1.5 million including fees at a Fair Warning auction in New York on Sept. 17, 2026, setting an auction record for McQueen.

“He was going for something that was entirely new,” says Brownawell. “This dress is a really prime example of that, the way that the print has been designed to lay perfectly within the architecture of the garment itself is really a spectacular sort of couture level of creation. On top of that, you have this unbelievably architectural draping, which, you know, McQueen has, it’s been said that he really actually draped a lot of these pieces directly onto the forms themselves because it was so complex.”

Aside from the dress itself, Alexander McQueen’s spring/summer 2010 show was ahead of its time in every way. It was the first show to be livestreamed in real time on the internet, and it was the first fashion show to debut a major pop single during a show; Lady Gaga’s “Bad Romance” premiered during the show’s finale. “McQueen’s legacy has been just growing stronger and stronger every year,” adds Brownawell.

The dress is hitting the auction block at a time when Christie’s is launching its inaugural fashion auction. “We really believe that the market is at a point right now where people do appreciate the important designs,” he says. “There’s a lot of clothing out there, but there’s also a lot of very important pieces that define what we wear and where fashion is going and where it’s been.”

#6641. The New Rules of Electric Vehicle Ownership

You have a keen eye for a fashionable investment—whether it’s a vintage accessory, a high-quality classic, or a trendy piece to keep your wardrobe current. But your closet isn’t the only arena that’s kept up to date. With your finger on the pulse of all things elegant and practical, no doubt the latest and greatest in personal transportation—electric cars—is firmly on your radar. This automotive upgrade is a step toward the future, and, like all new things, comes with some specific guidelines. With the help of State Farm, we’ve outlined what to consider before you elevate your status to EV owner—from how the flexibility of an EV factors into your routine, travel plans, and commute to how best to protect your fabulous new asset.

When choosing an EV, consider how it fits into your lifestyle. Location, budget, and driving habits should all play a role in finding the right fit. For example, if you spend a lot of time on the highway, a hybrid may make more sense than an all-electric model since you’ll have gas as a backup when your battery runs low. You’ll also want to think about how much passenger and cargo space you need—if you’re regularly hauling people, pets, or plenty of (literal) baggage, compare the costs of larger models that can accommodate everything comfortably.

You love vintage, but does that extend to your car? It just depends on your needs.

When deciding to buy pre-owned or new, think about how long you’re looking to own the car. Consider battery wear and how much it costs to replace one, your total budget (including financing, maintenance, and insurance), and whether or not you’re eligible for any tax credits that could offset the price of a new EV.

Yes, you’re already envisioning yourself pulling onto the street in your fabulous new ride, but make sure you weigh the pros and cons to save yourself from buyer’s remorse later.

You passionately curate your life, and the same should go for your electric car’s coverage. When considering insurance, EVs require a bit of what non-electric cars need, along with a few additional protections.

Protecting yourself and your investment starts with liability, collision, and comprehensive, just like with traditional cars. But with an EV, you’ll also need to cover battery damage, charging equipment, and specialized repairs. As a result—and because of higher purchase prices, specialized parts and repairs, and more—pricing tends to be higher than on policies for traditional cars. Manage these costs by comparing quotes on the model you choose, taking advantage of discounts for anti-theft devices and safe driving records, and, if you can help manage the potential out-of-pocket cost, adjusting your deductible a bit higher to lower your monthly payments.

You don’t need to do this all alone, though. Just like you’d turn to a trusted friend for a second opinion on your outfit, State Farm is there to answer your EV insurance questions and offer you an insurance quote before you buy.

When shopping for an EV, think about how far you’ll typically drive, where you’ll charge, and how long charging will take. Most EVs can go around 200 miles on a full charge at lower city speeds, but your charging setup matters, too. If you’re planning to charge at home, you’ll want to factor in installation of a charger, electricity costs, and potential homeowners insurance considerations. If you’ll rely on public chargers, make sure there’s a reliable network along your usual routes. It’s also worth knowing what kind of charger your car uses: Level 1 chargers plug into a standard outlet and can take up to 24 hours, while Level 2 chargers use a 240-volt outlet and offer a faster, more convenient option for home charging.

Much like you carry a purse-sized mending kit for fashion fixes, it’s always good to have an EV backup plan for automotive emergencies.

Add EV-specific roadside assistance to your insurance plan.

Collision or comprehensive insurance could cover this, or your warranty may cover normal degradation.

After your deductible payment, collision or comprehensive coverage should help lower costs.

The answer varies by model, so do your research, but know that you can add gap insurance or new car replacement to your plan to mitigate the issue.

Material: CalfskinLining: LambskinCarry options: Key snap hookClosure: Zipper with a silver-finish metal D stirrupInterior: Space for keys and a credit card

The Bow bag in Newspaper Print builds on one of the Maison’s longstanding motifs. Anderson brings that history into a new accessory, gathering supple lambskin into a sculptural bow-shaped silhouette. The Newspaper motif adds another archival reference, while the chain strap, finished with bow details and a leather insert, extends the design across the hardware. The result is a small bag with a strong shape and a clear connection to Dior’s visual language. It can be worn over the shoulder or carried by hand as a clutch, making it particularly useful for dinners, cocktail parties, and formal events when a large everyday bag would feel out of place. First introduced in 1999, the Saddle bag takes its shape from the equestrian world. Its asymmetrical flap recalls a saddle, while the D-shaped hardware references a stirrup clasp. The design has become one of the brand’s most recognizable silhouettes, appearing in different materials, colors, and patterns over the years. This bag gives the familiar shape a graphic update, pairing the archival black-and-white motif with calfskin construction and silver-finish hardware. The print makes the curved silhouette stand out, so the bag can anchor an outfit rather than simply complement it. The best graphic print accessories are the ones that complement your wardrobe and suit how you dress. A patterned bag is an easy starting point because it adds visual interest to familiar outfits, while a printed wallet, scarf, or key case offers a subtler way to try the trend. If you want a piece you can wear often, look for a print with colors that already appear in your closet. Consider scale, too: bold, oversized graphics make a stronger statement, while smaller, more repetitive patterns tend to feel understated.

Start with the accessory’s dominant colors. A black-and-white print works with denim, solid-color knitwear, tailored separates, and simple dresses. If you want to introduce another pattern, look for a shared color or vary the scale so the prints don’t compete. You can also coordinate your shoes or belt with one of the colors in the accessory for a more pulled-together look.

Think about both function and form. For work, choose a structured tote or a compact bag with enough room for your daily essentials. For travel and errands, a crossbody bag keeps your hands free, while a small pouch or printed card holder adds pattern without taking up much space. For weddings, dinners, and parties, a clutch or small shoulder bag can make more of an impact. The most versatile choice is one that suits the occasion without sacrificing the storage or carrying options you need.

Let the bag be the main patterned accessory. Solid colors, denim, and clean tailoring give a graphic print room to stand out. If you wear printed clothing, choose a pattern that shares a color with the bag or has a different scale. You don’t need to match every accessory; a few complementary pieces are usually enough to make the outfit feel cohesive.

#6639. Meet the Stylists Who Shaped Vogue’s Best-Dressed List

In case you missed it, Vogue’s 2026 best-dressed list has officially arrived—and on it are plenty of well-clad celebrities driving fashion forward.

While all of these A-listers come with their own distinct sense of style, their masterful stylists have played an important role in making them true red-carpet stars. As they say, “it takes a village”—so let’s pour one out for the amazing fashion minds who help craft all of the glamorous moments.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Kendall Jenner, Carey Mulligan, Greta Lee, Ayo Edebiri.

Styling approach: “My approach is always client-first. It’s important to me that what they wear on the red carpet feels authentic to who they are.”

Favored silhouette: “I’m really drawn to silhouettes that feel a little unexpected and challenge convention, but still translate naturally to the red carpet.”

Most-pulled accessory: “A Sophie Buhai teardrop pouch.”

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Connor Storrie.

Styling approach: “I always start with the person rather than the clothes. For me, great styling is about understanding someone’s personality, proportions, and how they carry themselves, then building on that. With Connor, I’ve always drawn heavily on Old Hollywood, particularly the 1920s and 1930s, bringing those references into something that feels contemporary and a little unexpected. I want the clothes to enhance the person rather than overpower them. There’s nothing better than a beautifully executed look that feels completely effortless.”

Favored silhouette: “I’m really drawn to a strong shoulder, a slightly higher waist, and a beautiful, long, wide-leg trouser. There’s something incredibly flattering and seductive about those proportions. I love the elegance of traditional menswear, but with a slightly louche, almost 1970s sensibility. It’s masculine without feeling rigid, and there’s a real sense of movement and ease to it.”

Signature touch: “I think my strength is understanding proportion and knowing when to hold back. I’m much more interested in personal style than chasing trends. Sometimes the smallest adjustments to a jacket, the way a trouser falls or how a shirt sits against the body can completely transform a look. I also love finding that balance between classic elegance and a little sex appeal. Nothing should ever feel forced or as though someone’s wearing a costume.”

Most-pulled accessory: “Pinky rings. I know they’re having a real moment on the red carpet, particularly in menswear, but they’re something I find myself coming back to. Even for Connor’s most recent red carpet at the Academy Museum Gala, convention might suggest wearing just one, but we loved both Tiffany & Co. rings so much that we decided to wear one on each pinky. One was a platinum ring featuring a cat’s-eye alexandrite surrounded by diamonds, while the other was a platinum ring set with a diamond of over eight carats. Two insanely beautiful pieces, and rather than choosing between them, we thought, why not wear both? I love those little moments where you go against the grain. Sometimes breaking an unwritten fashion rule creates something far more interesting and unexpected, and therein lies the fun of styling!”

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Teyana Taylor, Colman Domingo.

Styling approach: “Firstly, we consider the event and where our client is at that time in their career to decide what feels right for the moment. It’s also dependent on what our clients feel best in—making sure that they feel their truest and most confident self. Then, between the two of us, we also have to have synergy and feel good about a look, which we almost never disagree on.”

Favored silhouette: “As we like to say—never waste a waist! We always love cinched-in jackets, corsets, and waistlines and are so happy to see them being modernized on both the runway and red carpet at the moment. Right now we are seeing waistlines highlighted through accentuated peplums, exaggerated hips, and snatched bodices.”

Signature touch: “Jewelry is beyond important to us and always makes a look feel finished. Whether it’s diamonds, colored stones, or metal-based pieces, we love to use jewelry to elevate or put a twist on a look that might otherwise feel expected.”

Most-pulled accessory: “We always gravitate towards a Christian Louboutin So Kate pump for our female clients, or the Christian Louboutin Ziggissimo heeled boot for our male clients.”

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Tessa Thompson, Whitney Peak.

Styling approach: “I think about the project, the event, and what we are communicating. But ultimately, I’m thinking about the woman I’m dressing, and what we have established as a fashion identity. And what makes them feel amazing.”

Favored silhouette: “I’m not sure this defines my approach. When I see a look, it’s more that I connect it to a person. It’s much more organic and romantic than just saying, ‘Minis for spring!’”

Signature touch: “My signature touch is that my clients look like they all have the best style, and that the clothes never wear them.”

Most-pulled accessory: “I love a mega earring. And a perfect little sack clutch. I just want to be Mrs. Prada!”

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Olivia Rodrigo.

Styling approach: “Our approach is rooted in the individuality of each client, creating looks that feel authentic yet unexpected. We love refined and timeless silhouettes but always need a little edge, or elements that aren’t so perfect. Ultimately, we want every look to tell a story, feel effortless, and leave an impression.”

Favored silhouette: “We are really drawn to the two extremes right now—either something incredibly sculpted and structured, or fluid with beautiful draping. How a look moves, especially on the carpet, is so impactful.”

Signature touch: “Our signature touch is finding the balance between femininity and edge—we love taking something traditionally beautiful and introducing an unexpected element via a shoe, accessory, fabric, or silhouette.”

Most-pulled accessory: “Our most pulled accessory is often a rare or untraditional shoe! We don’t always use them, but we are obsessed with interesting shoes.”

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Rebecca Hall, Morgan Spector.

Styling approach: “I always start with the person rather than the clothes. Understanding who they are, what makes them feel confident, and how they want to be perceived is essential. When putting together a look, I’m already considering the final image. The clothes, accessories, and glam all play a part, as does the way the client carries the look, how they pose, and how it’s photographed. The best looks are a creative collaboration between stylist, glam, and the client.”

Favored silhouette: “Long column silhouette with a strong neckline.”

Signature touch: “Clean lines with a touch of drama or tension.”

Most-pulled accessory: “Black pointed toe pumps.”

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Daisy Edgar-Jones, Kendall Jenner

Styling approach: “I always say I try to see my client’s style, just through my eyes. It always starts and ends with them, and that excitement when our visions align is when the relationship is magic.”

Favored silhouette: “Knee-length skirts (even better if it’s a skirt suit), medium-sized bags, and square-toe heels—I can never get enough.”

Signature touch: “Chic and cool. That combo is always what underwrites my vision. I’m always drawn to looks that say something but are still timeless—that make a moment in one part being really interesting, and the rest being really fluid, classic, or refined.”

Most-pulled accessory: “Black satin slingback pumps and great sunglasses.”

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Louisa Jacobson.

Styling approach: “Thinking about who is being dressed, and the event they are attending, is paramount. Being ‘appropriately dressed’ (whatever that may mean) is important, but also keeping in mind who the client is and what they want to convey with their look. From there, as confirmations begin to roll in, I start to think about the type of jewelry that will complement the look, and I continue onwards with shoes and a bag. I really like to keep a tight edit of things, but make sure that the pieces all work well.”

Favored silhouette: “I’m all about tailoring. A beautifully-tailored suit is timeless in my opinion. However, it’s fun playing with different proportions and materials to keep it fresh.”

Signature touch: “I don’t know that it is unique per se, but I really want to make sure whomever I am dressing feels comfortable and super confident in their look. That is not to say I won’t suggest things that may be slightly out of their comfort zone—because I think that it’s important to try new things.”

Most-pulled accessory: “I tend to favor a simple shoe shape. I am a big fan of Gianvito Rossi’s Portofino and Elle styles. I tend to have both styles at just about every fitting, because they work so well.”

Comprising everything from tees and tanks to shorts and jackets, YPB reflects Abercrombie’s ability to evolve while staying true to its heritage. It’s also versatile enough to seamlessly move from a strenuous workout to the everyday wardrobe rotation. To put the collection through its paces, we’ve styled three looks that show just how far YPB can go.

I am a chronic overheater so my gym outfits always reveal a bit of skin. (It’s also a vanity thing so I can see my muscles at work when I’m getting after it.) This vintage-inspired muscle tank looks like some of the actual vintage tees that I’ve taken a pair of scissors to without a stranger’s set-in stains. I have a lot of hair that gets in my way so headwear is a must when working out. A bandana is a nice throwback to the classic bodybuilder era and unlike a hat, it does a better job at soaking up the sweat so it’s not dripping down my face.

The standout of this outfit is the shorts. Compression lined, they’re about as long as I’d go for shorts clocking in with a five-inch inseam. I’ve come to learn that recovery days are not only a blessing but a necessity. But they don’t necessarily mean you have to waste away on the couch all day. I can’t deny their comfort factor, and it’s hard to beat a sweater-and-shorts combo, an outfit beloved by my favorite A-listers.

The sweater was a quarter-zip with an elastic waistband for a more streamlined, tailored fit. And if I’m walking a little too briskly, the top easily comes off to reveal a staple graphic tee in my wardrobe.

Finally, I put on some pants! I don’t make it a habit to wear sweatpants out casually, but sometimes the weather calls for it. Hike ‘em up a bit and show off some crisp white socks, a style swerve I saw once and couldn’t help but copy.

The staple of this outfit is the heavyweight jacket. Its water-resistant lining keeps me dry when the meteorologists get the forecast wrong, and it’s lined to keep me warm as the days get shorter and the nights get longer. The two-way zipper also allows for some extra mobility, and it won’t bunch up when I sit down like so many other parkas.

#6635. An Ode to CVS, the American Answer to the French Pharmacy

Why this humble mainstay pharmacy is a favorite among celebrities, beauty editors, and TikTokers

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

According to my CVS Health app, I currently have 134 deals and rewards available based on my spending habits—several of which expire soon—and I’ve saved a not-small chunk of change since opening an ExtraCare account in 2008, when my love affair with the store began. While I probably wasn’t shopping for the exact same things back then, the surge of energy I get when walking through those sliding automated doors remains the same.

There’s something about the monotony of walking the aisles of CVS Pharmacy that helps regulate my nervous system, which is something I can’t say about my experiences in Europe’s widely beloved French pharmacies and British chemists. Don’t get me wrong: I’ll never miss an opportunity to restock Parisian cult-favorite skincare and rare beauty treatments not yet released in the States, but my intention behind those pharmacy trips isn’t quite the same. In Europe, I’m on a mission, but at CVS, I’m on pause. (In fact, CVS actually now carries a few French pharmacy staples … but I digress.)

The American pharmacy offers an outlet for retail therapy, temporary mindlessness, and reduced external overstimulation. There’s something downright meditative about the store’s harsh overhead fluorescent lights and ongoing scanner beeps; taking my time perusing everything from the latest hair accessories and nail-polish shades to discounted bags of Halloween candy, I always enter a state of relaxation. And I’m in good company. Both Rihanna and Law Roach have been spotted in the past month shopping for wellness essentials at the retailer. (Stars—they’re just like us!)

Law posted a video of himself entering CVS for a nasal decongestant spray and leaving with a haul that included cold Coca-Cola and a new Doritos flavor he’d never tried. “Have a good day, CVS shoppers!” he says as he leaves the store after ringing up his items. “That was so much fun. I’m a regular person.” Apparently, so is Kim Kardashian, who told radio personality and podcast host Angie Martinez earlier this year how much she misses visiting her local store. (Kardashian was even photographed at CVS with comedian and My Next Guest host David Letterman back in 2020.)

Dua Lipa, who grew up in London, also counts the retail destination as a must-have stop when visiting America. “I’m a little bit obsessed with CVS,” the star previously said in a Vogue interview. “That’s kind of like the mad shop that America has that I feel like has anything and everything. And so every time I come to the States, I’m like, right, first stop CVS, and I go and get my melatonin and some funky toothpaste and whatever kind of mad things I can find. There’s always something crazy and some weird-flavored crisp.” In recent years, CVS has leveraged the celebrity love, partnering with a few famous ambassadors, like Danielle Fishel, Selma Blair, and Kerry Washington.

According to a 2025 CVS Health report, about 8 in 10 American adults reportedly visited a pharmacy in the past year. So it’s not just me; CVS is woven into the fabric of American communities. A casual scroll through TikTok reveals hundreds of shopping hauls, coupon-stacking hacks, and unboxing videos dedicated to the retailer. (The store’s 12 Days of Beauty calendar is now sold out, but find additional options here.)

No matter what’s going on in my life, I know I can always step into a CVS and be soothed (not least because there are 9,000 locations). Besides, who can resist the ticker-tape-style receipts shoppers always get after a purchase, teeming with limited-time coupons and cash-back rewards? It’s a childlike delight, like a strip of arcade tickets won on Skee-Ball, beckoning me to come back soon. And I always do.

#6634. Vogue’s Best Dressed People of 2026

Our goal was 50—just 50!—of the best-dressed people of the year, a list to commemorate the unforgettable fashion moments of a very topsy-turvy 2026. Sounds easy…but, well, list-making never is. There were athletes who turned game days into runways, actors who owned the red carpet and the sidewalk, and method-dressing movie stars who artfully ignored the meaning of the word cut.

We wanted them all, plus some highly fashionable characters from unexpected fields and walks of life, and we wanted couples, which we insisted should be counted as singletons (a technicality!). We struggled and horse-traded and voted and arrived finally at…55! (The same number as last year.) Here is the fruit of our labor: an unranked, diligently categorized, highly subjective list of Vogue’s best dressed of 2026. And it all begins with our cover star, a selection that was the result of a rather heated debate. Enjoy!

Written by: Christian Allaire, Margaux Anbouba, Taylor Antrim, Max Berlinger, Laird Borrelli-Persson, Anna Cafolla, Liam Hess, Alexandra Hildreth, Hannah Jackson, Joan Kennedy, Irene Kim, Anna Grace Lee, Nicole Phelps, Madeleine Schulz, and Emma Specter.

STORRIE TIME Conner Storrie brings the Ken-ergy in a miniaturized version of his Gucci Best Dressed cover look. Coach watch pendant.

Why 2026 was his year: Playing brooding Russian hockey player Ilya Rozanov in the gay romance Heated Rivalry—in various states of deshabille—launched this 26-year-old Hollywood hopeful waiting tables in Los Angeles to cultural supernova. His last 12 months have seen a kind of fashion miracle: Storrie is now better known for what he wears than what he doesn’t. Click here for his cover-story conversation with Chloe Malle—which ranged from Storrie’s punk roots to his adoration of Parker Posey, his side hustle in “provocateur” photography, and more.

Friends, lovers, collaborators—occasionally all at once.

Why 2026 was their year: Him: Train Daddy in The Gilded Age; Her: Wicked stepmother in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story (and more).

Their couple style, in essence: Hudson Valley cabincore meets Tom Ford heat.

Kravitz wears The Row. Styles wears The Row and Adidas.

Their year in fashion: Excellent outerwear, statement headgear, rave-ready sunglasses, plenty of The Row.

Their couple style, in essence: Kiss all the time. Dress alike, more than occasionally.

From left: Imhof wears Balenciaga, Teuscher wears Rodarte; both wear Valentino.

Why 2026 was their year: Teuscher traded Lincoln Center for Hong Kong to star in her partner Imhof’s queer, Shakespearean House of Swans.

Their couple style, in essence: Berghain Romeo and Juliet.

Why 2026 was their year: Barone released comedy special Galaxy Brain; Skinner got to work on Overcompensating season 2. Together: their riotous podcast, Ride, and Halloween domination.

Their couple style, in essence: Newport Beach heartthrobs, if they canvassed for Zohran.

Left: Both in Dior. Right: Arquette wears Circus of Magdela; Lean wears Giorgio Armani.

Why 2026 was their year: Lean bringing down the house at the VMAs, while writing duets with Arquette; the couple hard-launching at Dior Men’s spring 2027 show.

Their couple style, in essence: Shades of blue (or bleu).

Left: Rosalía in Stella McCartney. Right: Bahia wears Saint Laurent; Rosalía wears Vivienne Westwood.

Their year in fashion: Contrasting-yet-coordinated masc-for-femme dressing, conjuring early days Justin and Hailey.

Why we can’t get enough: Two words: tooth necklace.

He said; she said: MGK to Vogue: “I started kind of respecting my upkeep, and I’ve watched things open up.” Johnson to Vogue: “[Musicians] like me, I don’t know what to say.”

Their couple style, in essence: Hoodies, diamonds, beanies, grommets, lace, leather, fangs. Misery business.

LIFE IN PLASTIC, IT’S FANTASTIC! Master of the step-and-repeat, Kendall Jenner set the gold standard for polka-dots in her Valentino Academy Gala dress.

The category is: great gowns, beautiful gowns.

Jenner wears Armani; Alexander Calder earrings.

Her year in fashion: Winged Victory at the Met, snagging ultra-rare Calder earrings for her first Lido, spreading the gospel of The Row, and perfecting polka dots at the Academy Gala.

Why we can’t get enough: She wears clothes like it’s her job.

Why 2026 was her year: Rose, Fatherland, and Project Hail Mary! (And, ahem, Digger.)

Highlight reel: Matières Fécales’ riff on the bar suit; Chanel’s riff on the hedgehog.

Her year in fashion: Dior standouts (acid green Poiret punk and impressionistic water lilies, specifically), plus an Issey Miyake breastplate, Marc Jacobs sequins, and Lii color blocking.

Best look of 2026: That star-spangled scarlet High Sport halter dress with a swishy fringed hem for the London premiere of Toy Story 5—a clever, playful wink to the film’s universe that still felt fashion.

Mulligan wears (from left): Colleen Allen; Dries Van Noten; The Row; Celine.

Why 2026 was her year: Lending her voice to Wildwood, scoring an Emmy nom for Beef season 2, getting a CBE from the King (she wore The Row).

Best look: That triptych of pixelated floral brocades from Julian Klausner’s fall 2026 Dries Van Noten collection. Bonus points for the pockets in the top!

Why this was her year: An awards-season run for Hamnet; an ultra-chic stint on the jury at Cannes.

Best look of 2026: Schiaparelli’s spiky “Isabella Blowfish” dress was a creepy-cheeky wow on the runway—and doubly satisfying on the Croisette.

A DOLL’S HOUSE Who says you can only wear your Met Gala dress once? Back in her Barbie Dreamhouse closet, Paloma Elsesser plays dress-up in her bespoke Bureau of Imagination gown.

They’re wearing your favorite brand—you just don’t know it yet.

Elsesser wears (from left): Junya Watanabe; Comme des Garçons, Phoebe Philo shoes, Chanel bag; Goyagoma.

Why 2026 was her year: When she wasn’t on the hunt for her next vintage deep cut? Hitting the runway for Ferragamo and Junya Watanabe and debuting Francesco Risso’s Bureau of Imagination at the Met.

She’ll get bragging rights for: The Bureau of Imagination gown—patchworked, painted, and embellished by “a squadron of people.” A true one-of-a-kind.

Thompson wears Giovanna Flores; Kallmeyer.

Why 2026 was her year: A Golden Globes nomination for Hedda; the runaway thriller His & Hers; and her Broadway debut in Fear of 13 alongside Adrien Brody.

She’ll get bragging rights for: Her support of all things indie is as evident in her work as in her wardrobe: just take the enviably cool Giovanna Flores patchwork dress she wore on a sweltering day in New York.

Peak wears (from left): Lii; Diotima; Torishéju.

Why 2026 was her year: She drummed up Hunger Games hype, toggling her looks between indie darlings and bona fide fashion-girl pulls.

She’ll get bragging rights for wearing: A scrunched-up black top and red cut-out leather skirt from London-based Torishéju; the standout textured Diotima dress from this season; and New York favorite Liii.

She’ll get bragging rights for wearing: A custom dress from Polimoda fashion school graduate Elias Matso, made entirely from steel boning and beads in a process that took over 300 hours.

Her year in fashion: Ditching goth—at least until Wednesday season 3.

OUT OF THE BOX On the lively streets of New York City, Sarah Pidgeon does her best CBK in a leopard-print Adam Lippes coat. Susan Alexandra pigeon charm.

Why 2026 was her year: She introduced a new generation to Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy—and her Yohji Yamamoto-filled closet—in Love Story.

Give her an Oscar for this look: The lacy aqua blue slip dress she wore to the Chanel Pre-Oscars party married CBK-ish ’90s minimalism with present-day Blazy-mania.

Why 2026 was her year: The Drama! Spider-Man! The Odyssey! Dune! Oh, and she found time to marry Tom Holland, too.

Give her an Oscar for this look: The white strapless Matières Fécales gown with matching feathered wings while promoting The Odyssey was pure Athena realness.

Edgar-Jones wears (from left): Miu Miu; Andreas Kronthaler for Vivienne Westwood; Rodarte.

Why 2026 was her year: The 18th-century-inspired Sense and Sensibility press tour, featuring a dreamy blush Galliano jacket worn with jeans; sexed-up pantaloon sets from Dries Van Noten and Colleen Allen; and lots and lots of Stella McCartney-era Chloé.

Up next: Going toe-to-toe with Michelle Williams in A Place in Hell and bringing another book club favorite to the big screen in Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow.

Robbie wears Schiaparelli; Dilara Findikoglu.

Why we can’t get enough: Schiaparelli couture with Elizabeth Taylor’s legendary Taj Mahal diamonds one day, cutoff jorts the next.

Up Next: How will she method-dress for Untitled Ocean’s Eleven Prequel?

Fanning wears (from left): Robert Wun; Givenchy by Sarah Burton; Evan Clayton.

Why 2026 was her year: Earned her first Oscar nomination for Sentimental Value, delivered Margot’s Got Money Troubles, and dressed in her Capitol best for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Her style, in essence: Anything can be a hat!

OFF THE SHELF Olivia Rodrigo, here in vintage Rudi Gernreich, brought major flower power with her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival. Susan Alexandra flower and mushroom charms.

Pop stars or politicians—they’re all headliners to us.

Why 2026 was her year: It was a legacy-defining one between Rodrigo’s best album yet (hello, seven Grammy nominations) and her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields music festival, which raised $20 million to support nonprofits for women and girls.

Her year in fashion: She joined a long line of badasses who’ve subverted the babydoll dress—Kathleen Hanna and Courtney Love come to mind.

Why we can’t get enough: From this summer’s ribbon-cutting at the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Thom Browne to attending the U.S. Open in red, white, and blue Chanel, she makes patriotism look chic.

The look that deserved a push notification: The Acne Studios skirt custom-printed with a photo of her late mother Marian Robinson, a gesture that brought the former president—and the rest of us—to tears.

Dion wears (from left): Tom Ford; Dior; Chanel; Chanel.

Why 2026 was their year: A triumphant return to the stage following her stiff person syndrome diagnosis meant 16 sold-out shows at Paris’s Plénitude Arena, plus daily pap walks outside of Le Royal Monceau.

The look that deserved a push notification: In Venice, a lesson in indie-darling dressing: Gucci skirt suit, below-the-knee tattoo, visible leg hair.

TINY FURNITURE Just like Mary, Cole Escola is the picture-perfect homemaker in the Christopher John Rogers jumpsuit they wore to the Tonys. Movado watch. Jennifer Behr earrings.

#6632. Noah Cyrus Delivers a Daring Take on Sister-of-the-Bride Attire

She chose a goth naked dress for Miley’s intimate nuptials this weekend

This past weekend, Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando tied the knot with an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California, where both the bride and groom wore Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello. For the occasion, Cyrus chose a silk boatneck maxi dress with an open back, while Morando wore a classic black tuxedo. And based on early photos from the ceremony, it appears that all of their guests were asked to stick to a black-and-white color scheme, too.

This was further evidenced late last night, when Cyrus’s younger sister, Noah, shared a series of Instagram photos showing off her gothic sister-of-the-bride ensemble.

For the wedding weekend, Noah chose a plunging scoop-neck maxi dress in black, made of a semi-sheer fabric that was decorated with jacquard florals. The body-hugging design featured cap sleeves and slight ruffles at the bottom of the skirt, and Noah paired it with a set of matching peep-toe heels, while layering a black blazer on top and matching panties underneath.

Later, based on photos she shared to her Instagram Story, it appears Noah switched into another black dress—a high-neck bodycon piece with a large silk sash tied into a bow along her waist.

Other members of Cyrus’s family who were in attendance included her mom, Tish, and her mother’s husband, Dominic Purcell, as well as Cyrus’s dad, Billy Ray Cyrus, and his girlfriend, Elizabeth Hurley. Miley’s older half-sister, Brandi, was also seen leaving the venue with her fiancé, Matt Southcombe. It is unclear whether Miley’s younger brother, Braison, or her half-brothers, Trace and Christopher, were present.

#6631. 2026 Was the Year of the Fashion Bride

If—for a certain set of cool, young designers—doing bridal was once thought uncool, 2026 may have been the year that finally put that notion to rest.

We’ve been seeing the shift for years now: For many brides, the wedding-day dream has gone beyond the beautiful, white, traditionally “bridal” wedding dress. Increasingly, brides want something, well, cool—an expression of their personal brand and sensibility, whether that means a painstakingly sourced archival look or a custom piece by an unexpected designer. This year, that trend was on full display, as wedding fashion increasingly became a stage and cultural touchpoint for brides and designers alike.

2026 was a banner year for high-profile weddings and celebrity brides wearing everything from romantic gowns to razor-sharp suits: Zendaya and Tom Holland, Dua Lipa and Callum Turner, Dove Cameron and Damiano David, Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez, Emma Roberts and Cody John, Karl-Anthony Towns and Jordyn Woods, to name just a few.

And that’s without even mentioning the “royal wedding” of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce. While the photos are yet to be released (and if you ask Swift bestie Dakota Johnson, they never will be), we do know that Swift became Jonathan Anderson’s first celebrity bride, a move that had people feverishly searching for clues at his Dior Haute Couture show in July. Could it be that white chiffon and degradé lace final gown, which later graced the runway at Vogue World: Milan? Nothing was revealed, apart from Anderson telling Women’s Wear Daily, “It was a joy to work with her. We became very good friends,” and “It’s an emotional thing doing someone’s wedding.”

Dua Lipa’s August wedding, meanwhile, was a fashion extravaganza, starting with a custom Schiaparelli white skirt suit, designed by creative director Daniel Roseberry. Who can forget the image of the pop star, beaming under a burst of confetti as she walked out of the town hall as a newlywed? Her suit was inspired by Bianca Jagger’s bridal look for her wedding to Mick Jagger in Saint-Tropez on May 12, 1971, perhaps the ultimate cool-girl bridal nod. Lipa rounded out her bridal looks with a white leather Bottega Veneta custom gown by Louise Trotter, and a Chanel haute couture gown for her main wedding dress.

Beyond the celeb wedding world, this year saw rising stars and in-demand designers put forward bridal looks, some for the first time. Dilara Findikoglu launched her first bridal capsule, a rule-breaking, lingerie-forward offering adapted from her ready-to-wear line, with campaign photos of models smashing plates, smoking, and mounting their grooms. (“I really believe that the power of my clothes is to bring out the uniqueness in someone,” Findikoglu previously told Vogue. “That’s exactly why they became Dilara Brides: to reveal the most unique version of who they already are.”)

Dilara Findikoglu’s debut bridal collection.

Batsheva debuted her first bridal collection at New York’s Bridal Fashion Week. Christopher John Rogers solidified his status as a sought-after designer for stylish brides, including Vogue fashion market director Naomi Elizée Blue, TikTok brand strategist Ali Lebow, and film director Pam Nasr. In an interview with The New York Times about his rising profile in the wedding world, Rogers even teased his very own bridal collection.

Naomi Elizée Blue in Christopher John Rogers.

CFDA/Vogue Fashion Funders Zoe Gustavia Anna Whalen and Miss Claire Sullivan created custom bridal looks for Architectural Digest senior design editor Hannah Martin and the artist Tourmaline, respectively. Martin’s gown was inspired by a look from Whalen’s spring 2025 collection, featuring a corseted bodice with a padded hip. Whalen previously told Vogue about why she decided to take on a bridal client, a rare move for her. “It aligns so much with my general ethos of garments being these weighted, emotional objects,” Whalen said. “So when it’s the right fit, being able to create that with such intention for somebody else is so beautiful.”

Tourmaline (right) in Miss Claire Sullivan.

Elsewhere, Raul Lopez dressed his friends Juice Rodriguez and Cristal Veras in coordinated Luar for their New York wedding. Gabbriette became the first bride for Matières Fécales, the cult Paris label whose show Rihanna attended in September. And Colleen Allen, winner of the 2026 CFDA Emerging Designer of the Year Award, has quietly become the fashion girls’ dream wedding dress designer, after making a custom look for Charli xcx’s wedding reception last year.

“Bridal” no longer means just one thing. For independent designers, it can be a playground to express something new, a platform for their brand, and, as Joe Bobowicz observed in a Vogue Business article, a dependable revenue stream. And as people expand their ideas of what a wedding can look like—donning colorful gowns in every color from butter yellow to pink to black, and playing with material and silhouette—as we head into 2027, the future of bridal style has never been more thrillingly uncertain.

#6630. A Comprehensive Guide to the Madness of The Hunting Wives Season 1

Here’s everything you need to know ahead of the second-season drop on Netflix this Thanksgiving

“Melodramatic” barely grasps the intense emotional roller coaster of The Hunting Wives. The Netflix soap opera/erotic thriller introduced the world to the small town of Maple Brook, Texas, where the world revolves around a small group of eccentric, gun-toting divas who disproportionately find themselves at the center of sinful controversies that range from infidelity to murder.

Inspired by May Cobb’s novel by the same name, The Hunting Wives follows Sophie O’Neil (Brittany Snow), a bright-eyed transplant from Massachusetts who moves to Maple Brook with her husband, Graham (Evan Jonigkeit), and young son. This is partly because Sophie accidentally killed someone during a night of drunk driving. But now, Graham works for Jed (Dermot Mulroney), the richest man in town, who is gearing up for a gubernatorial run. His wife, Margo Banks (Malin Akerman), is the hypnotizing beating heart of this small town, along with her crew of strong-willed “hunting wives.” Upon meeting her, Sophie is immediately bewitched by her stoic demeanor and magnetic charm.

Margo’s inner circle includes several shit-talking, heavy-drinking wives who spend their days gossiping or shooting boars. Two of Margo’s small army rank above the rest: Jill Thompson (Katie Lowes), the pastor’s wife who loves her 18-year-old basketball prodigy son, Brad (George Ferrier), a bit too much, and Callie, the sheriff’s wife, who is fiercely (delusionally?) loyal to Margo. Margo and Callie’s love is very much not platonic, but it’s repeatedly jeopardized, especially because Margo is enamored with Sophie. In short, Callie hates (and I mean hates) Sophie.

To understand the show, one thing needs to be made abundantly clear: Everyone is horny, and anything is fair game. Or almost anything. At the center of Maple Brook’s salacious tangle of relationships is Jed and Margo’s (mostly) open marriage. The two of them can sleep with as many women as they want, and I mean only women (a misogynistic arrangement, yes, but this is Deep South Texas, after all). This allows Jed as many trysts as he wants and permits Margo’s secret romance with Callie. This rule, however, doesn’t really stop her from doing whatever she wants when she wants. This is deadly apparent because she’s full-blown romantically involved with (checks notes) her friend Jill’s teenage son, Brad.

The first part of The Hunting Wives finds thrills in socialites at each other’s throats. They toss dagger eyes, pair them with biting insults, and let lust dictate most (if not all) of their decisions. Then, a real tragedy rattles the town. Brad’s real (age-appropriate) girlfriend, the sweet Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe), is found shot in the head in the forest near the town lake. Many viable suspects live in this crime-ridden town: Pete (Paul Teal), the youth pastor who cares too much about his teens; Jill, viciously protective of her son; and Margo, who, as I mentioned, is sleeping with teenage Brad. The cops, however, only find signs pointing to the unassuming Sophie O’Neil, who spent the night at Margo’s nearby the night before and whose gun was confirmed as the murder weapon. (Uh-oh!)

The night of Abby Jackson’s murder, she leaves the lake party mad at Brad, who failed to show up because, well, he’s having sex with Margo. As the audience, we also learn that two prime suspects roam nearby: An angry Jill left the house to confront Abby, and creepy Pastor Pete parked his car nearby where he was … masturbating to a photo of Abby. But Margo invites Sophie over to her lake house for a night of fun. Without telling Sophie, Margot also invites Brad and his friend, Jamie (Chosen Jacobs), another 18-year-old who has the hots for Sophie—what a disaster! That night, Margo and Sophie share a kiss during Spin the Bottle, sparking one of the most co-manipulative relationships in TV history. On top of it all, they mix Xanax and alcohol, so no one remembers anything. This is troubling when Sophie wakes up alone on the dock with no memory and no gun.

We know Sophie’s gun was used to kill Abby—and she certainly had opportunity. But she had no motive whatsoever. Margo, on the other hand, has all three; Abby discovered Brad and Margo’s affair and threatened to expose it (an affair that, of course, had yielded an unplanned pregnancy and a subsequent abortion). And, in a frantic attempt to keep her wealthy lifestyle intact, she shoots Abby. But that was only the beginning. Margo first attempts to frame Sophie for the murder, but because she holds a soft spot for her, she instead decides to frame Jill, planting Abby’s phone in her house and twisting the story to her liking.

At this point, it’s essential to talk about what happened to Abby’s mother, Starr, who is often bullied by the popular clique of high-powered women. After Abby dies, Starr thinks Brad is the culprit, having seen the two of them engaged in a fight, but she changes her mind after she’s incorrectly told Abby’s had an abortion (it was Margo), and she thinks that Jill killed Abby to protest Brad. That’s when Starr, in a fury, drives to Jill’s with a shotgun in tow, only to get mowed down by the gun-toting pastor’s wife in an act of self-defense.

Jill emerges victorious from her spar with Starr, but it doesn’t last long. The cops start looking at her as the prime suspect because she was the last incoming call on Abby’s phone (and she had a motive). Margo, obviously knowing that’s not the case, accompanies Callie to confront Jill anyway, only to find Starr dead in the kitchen. That’s when Jill pulls a gun on them (this is crazy, I know), and Callie shoots first, killing her. This is also, in some way, a twisted act of love.

As all the shooting is going on, an off-duty cop follows a red herring in the form of Pastor Pete. (Yes, everyone is a little evil in Maple Brook, but he might be the most sinister resident of them all.) Deputy Wanda Salazar (Karen Rodriguez) has a feeling that the pastor isn’t who he says he is and is hiding a dark past. Thinking he is Abby’s murderer, she chases him down, only to find that he’s kidnapped two other girls, Kaycee and Nina, hauling them in a trailer behind his car. What the hell is in the water in this town!?

By the eighth episode, it seems Sophie has perhaps drunk too much of this Maple Brook water. She pieces together that Margo is the killer—and that she manipulated the situation to frame her for murder. Instead of going straight to the authorities (like any normal person might), she confronts Margo. This, of course, gives Margo enough time to alert her crazy, crack-smoking brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), who pops up as a nuisance throughout the series. Taking on the role of a protective older brother, Kyle tries to run Sophie off the road and intimidate her. What does she do? Run him over and kill him … so, no use going to the authorities anymore. In true Maple Brook fashion, she hides the body instead. And, yes, after all that, we’re ready for season 2, because now everyone’s a killer.

We will see what’s next for this sinister Texan town on November 26.
