#6629. Gordon Ramsay’s Routine for a Six-Pack at 60 Includes Daily Crunches and Red-Light Therapy

Gordon Ramsay has earned 17 Michelin stars throughout his career and still oversees nearly 100 restaurants. He also fronts prime-time TV franchises on both sides of the Atlantic and holds a couple of casual Guinness World Records (call him if you need to fillet a 10-pound fish in 1 minute five seconds).

This is a man who’s never met a goalpost he didn’t want to surpass. So it wasn’t entirely surprising when he posted a bare-chested shot of his six-pack to the grid earlier this month. What generated headlines was the occasion: his 60th birthday. “Gordon Ramsay thirst trap was not on my bingo card,” reads one comment. “My wife is on this app sir,” reads another.

At home in London, he shows me the Insights section on his Instagram account, which reveals the photo has gotten over 62 million impressions. “It’s very strange,” he says. “I’ve had a lot of ribbing from my eldest daughter, Megan. She’s a police officer. She was like, ‘Dad, how can you do that to me?’ All her senior sergeants and officers were laughing and telling her to tell me they’re going for a run. They’re in their early 40s. And then my Royal Marines Commando son just sent me a message with: ‘WTF dad, what are you doing?’”

Ramsay has been a pretty active guy for a while now, despite working in an industry typically associated with chaotic diets and zero time for exercise. He was a youth soccer player back in the day, before becoming a chef and then, in his 40s, going from weighing 252 pounds to competing in marathons and Ironmans.

All very impressive, but it’s even rarer to be this chiseled in your 60s (maintaining a low body fat percentage becomes harder as your testosterone and growth hormone production slows down). Read on to learn more about his preferred forms of cardio, his favorite pre-workout treat, and why he's established a daily cryotherapy routine. “I call it my freezer,” he says.

“15 minutes a day. It starts off with a quick two-minute stretch and 100 sit-ups every morning. Precore lifestyle is my ab cruncher thing—these things are fucking amazing, by the way. If I miss a day, then I have to punish it and do double the next day.”

“It’s not physically hard with big weights. These are 25 pounds. I’ll do a strength class once a week, 45 minutes. That’s it. Occasional push-ups and squats. No personal trainer.”

“What’s helped tremendously, with no impact on any of the joints, is a lot of swimming. So I have an injury in my patella, my right knee, currently. So I just increased the swimming because that’s the only sport that can use every muscle in your body with zero impact. But cardio is off the charts.”

“I have a Zwift bike, so I jump on that for 45 minutes. There’s no impact on that. I’ll do that Monday, Wednesday, Friday and gear up for 90 minutes on a Sunday. If I wasn’t injured, I’d be doing three 5K runs again, Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 20-minute runs. I’ve got my 5K back down to 21 minutes. The dream is under 20. I was running at 19 and a half back in July. A 5K run is easy to do in the morning before work, it’s done within half an hour. Once I do that, I can gear up for either a two-hour bike on a Sunday or a 90-minute run. I alternate. So, one Sunday’s run, one Sunday’s bike.”

“10 years ago, I ruptured my Achilles. I invested in an AlterG, a beautiful running machine that takes your weight, so you get all the cardio you want and less impact on the joint.”

“From the chef’s perspective, I call it my freezer. It’s the cryochamber. I do two sets of three minutes every morning. I try to go seven days a week in that thing, straight after [working out]. That is incredible. That’ll get up to like minus 160. For six minutes.”

“I’ve invested in a tiny little red-light therapy sauna outside in the garden, and it seats two of you, and so [I’ll do] half an hour of that, every other day. This doesn’t need to be done every day. Three times a week’s fine. So when I’m not running, the other day I’ll sit in that red-light therapy and spend 20 minutes, 30 minutes in there, which is brilliant.”

“The older you get, the more you have to stretch. I use a lot of bands. And so after sitting and stretching, I had those incredible bands where you lift your feet up and pull and stretch. 5 minutes is always a nice stretch before you [work out] and then 10 minutes stretch after that. I’ve never been to a yoga class in my life.”

“I’m big on oatmeal for breakfast, Monday to Friday. I indulge Saturday, Sunday. I will do [oatmeal with] blueberry compote, caramelized banana for my potassium, and then fresh blueberries on top with some—it sounds weird, but it’s delicious—hot honey.”

“I have my friends at Precision. I’ll do one of their gels before I start that 5K, a protein gel, 30 grams, and then that sees me through the whole 45-minute routine. Coffee is just a full-fat, flat white, extra hot. Extra hot means I can sip it slowly. I cut out a lot of dairy, a lot of butter, a lot of cream. And so that treat in the morning with a flat white is that sort of, ‘I’ve earned this shit.’”

“I don’t overstress on that because I stay fit. I monitor what I eat, but if anything, I’ll do smaller portions now. I’ll involve a lot of spinach, involve a lot of salmon, chicken, especially thighs. We’re just smart with less cream, less butter intake. And then when we travel, we just keep it light.”

“I have a red wine with dinner, Californian, something light, something delicious. In 20, 30 years running restaurants, I’ve never gone around the room holding a glass of wine, holding a glass of champagne, sitting down, drinking with customers. Again, discipline.”

“Just a couple of spoons of creatine, five mornings a week. A little scoop in my water.”

“One thing I’ve learned in my 50s and my 60s—everyone said the older you get, the less you sleep. I think it’s the other way around. I like to be in bed by 11, and I’m up at 6. My Oura ring for me has become my best mate, because it just gives me the proper day-by-day indication and then keeps you on track for sleep.”

“Sign up for something. Have a target because that gets you out of bed, with a bigger, incentivized plan. I need that target twice a year, every six months. And I’ve done that since my 40th birthday. Whether it’s half an Ironman, whether it’s a marathon, half a marathon, I’ve always got something to focus on.”

“No, no, no, no, no, no. Definitely not. No. I mean, no. My meditation is Kitchen fucking Nightmares. Dealing with some of those contributors on there and having to sit with them and talk with them. But no, not very good at sitting still.”

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6628. The Art of the Winter Layer

Use these cold-weather staples from The North Face for practical warmth with polished style.

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Like any specialized skill set, winter layering is one that must be continually practiced and perfected, lest your talents wane. It’s not as easy as throwing on a pair of cashmere leggings and a coordinating hoodie—that’s only the beginning. From there, it takes a careful curation of hero pieces (like puffer jackets and parkas), as well as a cast of supporting details (hats, gloves, and high-performance footwear), to layer effectively and aesthetically in the harshest conditions.

That said, even the most adept artist is nothing without an arsenal of trusted creative tools. And in these bitter temps, you’ll want to reach for the best, which essentially means any piece of gear with The North Face’s iconic rectangular logo attached to it. The storied brand has dominated the outdoor space for decades, having perfected the art of elevated style at elevated altitudes.

As we head into the chilliest season of the year, look to The North Face’s vast selection of dependable staples for all your layering needs. Designed both for performance and appearances, these pieces are in it for the long run.

Whether painting or dressing, it’s essential to start any creative endeavor with a blank canvas made of quality materials. A good base should be versatile and simple to pair with a host of helpful staples. Long-sleeve tees, cashmere turtlenecks, and crewneck sweatshirts, for example, are all good jumping-off points.

If you’re looking for a high-performance piece with enough style power to stand on its own, we recommend the Women’s Chabot 2.0 Mock-Neck. This cozy layering top offers the same reliable comfort of a traditional insulated thermal with a few modern updates. Though understated by design, its delightfully oversized fit and a funky waffle knit texture make the basic feel intentional and interesting.

For a closer-fitting base, the Women’s Golden Ridge Ribbed Long-Sleeve Tee layers easily under other pieces. Its slim fit and ribbed texture give this practical layer a polished look, while thumbholes at the cuffs add a functional detail. Bonus points for the tee’s anti-odor technology that helps keep the fabric feeling fresh.

Women’s Golden Ridge Ribbed Long-Sleeve Tee

After you’ve selected the first layer, the next stop should be your coat closet. This is where you’ll select the hero of your look. While each piece of the layering puzzle is uniquely important, the power jacket is a non-negotiable. The right iteration should supply a thick layer of warmth, while also doing its part to make the outfit, as a whole, feel cohesive.

Those who crave a more subdued winter aesthetic will love the classic appeal of the Women’s Arctic Bomber. The waterproof winter jacket boasts all the utility of a parka, with the sleek design details most commonly found in trend-focused outerwear. In four comforting colorways, this winter coat is an insulation powerhouse in a chic, wearable package.

Look to the Women’s Hydrenalite Down Jacket for a more classic puffer. This work-horse is a versatile down layer that can be slipped on at any time to keep you warm for any duration that you spend outdoors, whether you are on the mountain or running around town.

For the more artistically inclined, try the Women’s Yumiori Off Peak Full Zip Jacket. This fleece outer layer offers unfailing warmth and a distinctly sporty flavor. Its two-tone color palette, meanwhile, adds a fun, whimsical feel to the utilitarian, zip-up-style silhouette.

During the summer months, it’s all about the mani-pedi. But once that icy weather blows in, self-care starts to look a bit different. The North Face’s Etip Gloves are basically a hand treatment on the go. Crafted from soft, stretchy fleece made with 93% recycled polyester, these tech-friendly gloves will keep your hands comfortable on cold-weather outings. They’ll also keep you connected: Touchscreen compatibility lets you check your phone without taking them off, while silicone grip dots on the palms help you hold onto your device as well as smaller essentials like keys and credit cards.

For footwear, the Women’s THERMOBALL Traction Mule V will quickly become the standout of your seasonal lineup. These cloud-like slip-ons pair warm insulation with a quilted upper that gives them a casual, streetwear-cool vibe. The rubber outsole adds traction for quick trips outdoors.

The minimalist philosophy requires you to take off one item before leaving the house. But during the cold weather season, it’s in your best interest to do the opposite. As you walk out the door, make sure you grab a beanie since most of your body heat can escape from your head.

Beanies are simultaneously the most underappreciated outfit addition and the most indispensable. The North Face’s Wool Blend Beanie, for instance, pairs the warmth of its 65% merino wool knit with a refined, metropolitan style. Its classic cuffed design and textured knit add visual interest, while its deep fit offers roomier coverage. If you prefer the rectangular logo with the same cuffed look, you can never go wrong with the rib-knit and soft lining of the Salty Lined Beanie. On the slopes or on your morning commute, either will add a polished finishing touch.

The importance of a functional winter hat cannot be overstated—think of it as the final brushstroke in the art of winter layering.

#6626. Bella Hadid’s Radical Vulnerability

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

How do you stay open in an industry that demands toughness? Bella Hadid embarks on a new chapter with a renewed sense of optimism and her boundaries firmly in place.

I first met Bella Hadid on a fashion shoot I was styling more than a decade ago. We went on to shoot several stories together, including her first major American magazine cover. On one of those shoots, she arrived upset because she had just found out she didn’t get cast in the Victoria’s Secret show. I will never forget telling Bella that one day, Victoria’s Secret would be begging her to walk for them. Cut to today, and Bella is not only one of the most in-demand models, but she opened their most recent show. When I saw her hit the runway in a beaded floral bra and matching wings, I let out a scream because I knew what that moment meant to her.

A few days after the Victoria’s Secret show in October, Bella and I sat down to reflect on her career so far, forgiveness and success, turning 30, and where she goes from here. I have always felt connected to Bella because she, like me, is a heart-on-her-sleeve kind of gal. She is deeply vulnerable and human, and it’s what makes her one of the most compelling figures in fashion today.

Samira Nasr: This is a full-circle moment. On one of our first shoots together, you were really upset because you didn’t get the Victoria’s Secret show. And I said to you, “One day, they will be begging you to be in their show.” And I could tell you didn’t believe me. Your whole body shut down. And three days ago, you opened Victoria’s Secret. Holy shit.

Bella Hadid: I still don’t believe you, to be honest. I feel like people are just AI-ing me onto the runway. I think that it’s so crazy how time passes and you still have some kind of impostor syndrome. No matter how hard you work, there’s always another girl who is more deserving, more beautiful, and has worked so hard to be able to get that spot. Ten years ago, I remember that moment too, where I never thought I would get the show, but I think that God always has a plan, and I truly believe at that time I wasn’t ready. I don’t think I’ve been ready until this year, to be honest. In past years, I was going to my horse-show finals in the morning, flying straight to the Victoria’s Secret show that day, doing rehearsal right before, and then pulling what we call a Bella, and Belinda comes out, and we just act. But this year, I felt really strong.

I have had to make a decision for myself to have boundaries with my own health. And I think it’s gotten me to this point now where I’m able to do the jobs that I do want to do with people that I love, that I can feel inspired by. And that’s truly what [working in] fashion is about: being around people you feel inspired by. Until you find that inspiration, it’s hard to go back into our industry. I think I needed a little bit of time just to be able to be like, “Let me just remember why I’m doing this again,” because I know I’m more than just a face.

SN: We don’t really support a culture of care. I have always believed that boundaries are bridges.

BH: They really are. We know so many people who have been working for 30, 40, 50 years in this industry with zero boundaries. I’ve watched people over the years just get more depressed because they don’t know themselves and they don’t know who they are. And that’s how I was for 10 years, when I didn’t know what my favorite color was, what I liked to eat. I stopped listening to music. To not be able to know yourself in an industry that tells you how to be every single day is really hard.

SN: Going back to Victoria’s Secret, did you feel empowered, or was that your alter ego? What is her name again?

BH: Belinda. You know what? Fortunately and unfortunately, I think it was Bella this year.

BH: I made up my alter ego, Belinda, a long time ago to deal with the intensity of everything happening in my life. So she could deal with that, and I can deal with this, and we can do this together, which I’m realizing I should probably go to therapy about again. Belinda is the one that people are like, “Wow, this, that.”

I have POTS [postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome], and I have a lot of PMDD [premenstrual dysphoric disorder], endometriosis, plus my Lyme and things that affect my body very deeply. Right before I walked out on the runway for my opening look, I went to go stretch and my whole clavicle completely … I don’t even know what it was. My lungs almost collapsed, and I couldn’t breathe, and then it was like, “Five, four …” So my body goes through these different motions of feeling really good and then all of a sudden crashing on me at the worst moments. I need to realize maybe my body can’t handle all that I have going on. Because I know how to walk. One thing I can do is I can strut. But it’s a lot of pressure; we all have our own insecurities. Sometimes my body just can’t connect with my brain. My brain wants to do it, and my body is like, “No, we can’t do that today.” And I’m like, “Okay, great. So let’s figure out another way.” But I think people don’t realize how much I struggle with the fatigue and the body pain, and so I just try my best.

SN: You’ve achieved so much in your 20s. You just turned 30. What are you looking forward to in your 30s?

BH: It’s funny, today I woke up with—I wouldn’t say the word is anxiety, but this feeling of “Oh my gosh, my life is starting.” I want to get rid of what doesn’t bring me joy and bring in what does. I’ve tried to put myself in positions for work for a very long time that have made me feel out of body or like I don’t belong. Years ago, I was just grateful to get a job, and I would say yes to everything. I lacked boundaries then, but I do believe that that gave me the strength to be able to have the confidence in my own boundaries now. I’ve achieved pretty much all the goals that I wanted to when it comes to fashion as a model. And now I do want to go into other ventures to eventually get to peace and happiness and love within this universe that God has put me in.

In the next couple of years, it’s just about getting back to community, getting back to using my voice again. I got beaten down pretty heavy for a long time, which pushed me into this very big struggle with my physical and emotional health, which makes my brain turn off and makes me not be able to write or read. When you’re not around enough people that are like-minded, you feel really ostracized. That’s almost where I got to. Of course, I always want to speak from my heart, which I hope will never disrespect anybody, but still be able to have the confidence to speak my truth and hope that people will walk beside me along the way when it comes to that.

SN: Is there something you’re most proud of achieving?

BH: Well, first and foremost, starting [my fragrance line] Orebella was something that I truly needed for my own creativity and to be able to build community. I am not a 50/50 person. I’m an all-in type of girl. Being able to move forward into my 30s, really focusing on building the things that I’ve started—Orebella was something that I pushed so hard for since 2018, and the fact that it’s really now coming to fruition makes me so proud.

When I was 17, going to my first go-see with a stylist I will not name, I was basically told I was too big to wear Saint Laurent and needed to lose a couple of pounds. And that’s when I was just a baby coming out of high school. Twelve years later, now I’m the face of Saint Laurent. I’m the face of Prada, which is incredible and insane. Times have changed so much, and the people that have come into the industry to make it a better place for us as models are so important. Not that that comment ever impacted me. I went through enough struggles with my body before that, so by the time she said that, I was like, “Okay, girl, I’m actually coming out of something that I dealt with very heavily when it came to my body. And now I look at food in a different way, and I love my body, and that’s okay if you think that I don’t look the way that you think I should look.”

I just would love for everyone to think about if every day they had to walk outside and be photographed, what that would feel like, because it’s an uncomfortable feeling for anybody. My face would change so much. I would be super puffy one day, and one day I would look yellow and emaciated, and people would think I was on drugs or doing this or that. And when anybody knows about, one, hormones, just as a woman in general, and two, about immune problems and how weight fluctuates—again, I just think that there needs to be more sensitivity in our industry.

SN: I’m curious if you’ve always been this person—so sensitive, empathetic—from a little girl.

BH: I’ve always felt like my sensitivity and my openness were a disservice to myself because I felt like no one else was like me in those ways, so I shut it down. Now I realize that there is a generosity of thoughtfulness that is so much deeper than just buying somebody an expensive gift. I think sitting on the side of the street with somebody, even if you don’t have any money, is more important than just walking by without caring.

SN: You’re able to access compassion when a lot of people can’t, and that is a superpower. I want to talk about style because you mentioned your archive. I remember you once mentioned you collect Gaultier. Do you still collect?

BH: I do collect. Behind me are bags to sell. But downstairs, I have my Gaultier dress that the atelier made. It was a Naomi Campbell dress that she had worn in one of their shows, and I was obsessed with it. I called their PR, and within a week and a half, because that dress was in a museum, I had it made and sent to Cannes, and that was that white-and-black dress that I wore on the carpet. And so, that’s here. My Coperni dress is here. I have a whole section for Virgil [Abloh].

SN: The last time I saw Virgil was with you, actually.

BH: I don’t think I’ve done a real, full Fashion Month since he passed away. And Vivienne [Westwood] and Karl [Lagerfeld] passed, and I felt like all of my idols were leaving, and it felt really scary. I have all the art Virgil gave me, his letter he wrote me, his bags, his shoes he made me. And then I have my Prada area, my Cavalli area, my Bob Mackies that I’ve been collecting over the years.

BH: Hopefully for a future wedding. There are just some dresses you can’t find again. And Bob did it best.

SN: He’s an American icon. I wanted to talk to you about Cannes. You’re such a queen of Cannes now, and I look forward to seeing you there. Is it fun?

BH: This past year was fun. I felt grounded. To do the red carpet and feel, in those moments, sober and happy and healthy and strong, and go to sleep not having anxiety about going out or how I’m going to look the next day, and just being with loved ones. It did really well for me this year.

Cannes has always held a very special place in my heart. It begins long before I arrive. Working closely with designers on custom gowns, exchanging references, and watching those first sketches come to life is such a beautiful part of the experience.

This year, being there to support Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Ben’Imana, the first Rwandan film in the official selection, was especially meaningful. It explores memory and reconciliation after the genocide against the Tutsi through women whose lives carry its legacy. That’s what I love about cinema: It brings us closer and gives stories too rarely heard the attention they deserve. You can enter a theater knowing nothing of someone’s world and leave carrying a little of it with you.

SN: I look at you and how hard you’ve worked for so long, from our first job together. To me, it feels like you’ve achieved so much. But what does success look like for you? Do you feel you’ve achieved it?

BH: I talked to my business manager yesterday, so that made me feel a little bit more successful. But when you don’t think about the money part of it, I think success truly comes from peace within. At the end of the day, I really don’t need much. That’s why I do give back so much, because a lot of the money that I do make, I don’t feel deserving of. There are so many people in the world, whether it’s doctors or teachers, that I think deserve my pay rate a lot more than I do.

From an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion shows you do. And that is really important in our industry, especially when you’re building. But for me, I am different. Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals. I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community. I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother. It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me. My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it.

I think knowing there is a reason behind everything is so important. My sister and I donated a million dollars to Palestine last year [the donation was split between HEAL Palestine, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, World Central Kitchen, and United Nations Relief and Works Agency], which we could have never been able to do without the success that we’ve had.

God gave me the platform to be able to speak about the things that I hold dearly to me. And when it comes to Palestine or Sudan or Congo or Rwanda or places that mean so much to not only myself but the people around me—to give people a voice in any capacity, that’s success for me as well. To make my family wide and far proud, or to see themselves in me, it gives me strength.

This story appears in the Winter issue of Harper’s Bazaar.

#6625. A Brief Guide to Grand Theft Auto VI’s Nike Sneaker Dupes

GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do. We’d already spotted Air Force 1 dupes in the trailers, but now that we can finally play the long-awaited masterpiece itself, we’re taking a closer look at what else is on the shelves. There are tons of different sneaker stores sprinkled throughout the game, and Eris—Rockstar’s fictional answer to Nike—has given us a lot to work through.

Even the name is a joke. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery. The Swoosh has been replaced with a pointier, upside-down logo, and plenty of the sneakers baring the mark are instantly recognizable.

The Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point. It’s the game’s AF1 equivalent, complete with the familiar paneled upper, perforated toebox, and a big, beefy sole underfoot. The Eris Strife 360, meanwhile, looks straight out of the Air Max 97 catalog. There’s the rippling upper, rounded toe, and long cushioning window underneath. Designed by Christian Tresser and released in 1997, the IRL sneaker’s silhouette took inspiration from water ripples, while the OG “Silver Bullet” finish drew on mountain bike components. Eris keeps enough of that shape for you to be able to spot it from across the shop.

Some versions get even more specific. There’s a white-and-orange Strife 360, for example, with oversized branding, contrasting lace loops, and printed side text that recalls Off-White’s own Air Max 97s. It isn’t a straight one-to-one recreation, but the reference feels pretty clear. An apparent take on the Off-White Air Force 1 Mid also appeared in the teasers. Someone at Rockstar is clearly a fan of Virgil Abloh’s work.

Then there’s the Eris Strife 90, with pairs that borrow heavily from the Air Max 90 “Infrared.” The bright red accents and sharp, aggressive lines are all there, with one colorway even adding black scribbles across the overlays.

Arguably the most iconic signature shoe of all time, the Air Jordan 1, gets a look in the game as well. The Eris Rook 1 High comes in leather and suede variations, with a tall ankle collar and laces running almost all the way up. There’s a black-and-white pair that swaps Jordan branding for an Eris basketball graphic on the tongue. You’ve probably got something quite similar in your closet at home.

The Eris Cross Trainers are, well, harder to pin down. Available in several colorways, they have a mesh base and leather overlays. One white-and-gray version gets bright green hits that nod to Nike’s signature “Volt” hue. The simpler construction puts it closer to an older Nike runner, somewhere around MD Runner 2 territory, than a direct Zoom Vomero 5 or V5 Rnr copy. And for those times that tying laces feels like too much work, there are the very appropriately named Eris Basic Slides. The broad branded strap and flat footbed are very Nike Benassi.

There are different versions to consider, too. “Origins” go all-white, while “Elite” options are matte and all-black. So if you‘ve found a silhouette you like, you can still spend another 10 minutes deciding which version works with your trousers. A problem we were hoping to leave outside the game.

It gives you an idea of just how much there is in GTA 6. The older games let you change your clothes, but here you’re choosing between different colorways, materials, and versions of individual shoes. And Eris is only one part of it: There are clothes and accessories that look like takes on Stüssy, Loewe, Chrome Hearts, and Louis Vuitton, too. You could spend a fair bit of time getting dressed before you get anything else done.

We’ve waited this long to play the game. A few more minutes in the sneaker shop before you really get going on missions won’t hurt.

A version of the story originally appeared on British GQ.

#6624. All That Glitters: Jewelry Highlights from Vogue’s Best Dressed List

When it comes to Best Dressed, it's not all about the threads, the baubles deserve their due, too. Scanning Vogue's illustrious 2026 list, we noticed that several of our honorees have a particular penchant for accessorizing, and an equally impressive command of the historical reference. Take Margot Robbie, who borrowed Elizabeth Taylor's Taj Mahal diamond for the Los Angeles premiere of Wuthering Heights, while Céline Dion revisited her own fashion history during her Paris residency, commissioning a new version of the Chanel Comète necklace she wore to the 1997 Oscars.

And the stories don't end there. From Colman Domingo's exuberant brooches to Zoë Kravitz's decidedly nonchalant approach to wearing enormous diamonds, this year's Best Dressed honorees know that jewelry can be as revealing of personal style as the clothes themselves. Whether it's a sentimental keepsake, a historical curiosity, or a spectacular feat of craftsmanship, these are the jewels that deserve a closer look.

For the Los Angeles premiere of Wuthering Heights in January, Margot Robbie paired her custom Schiaparelli gown with a piece of Hollywood history: Elizabeth Taylor's Taj Mahal diamond. The heart-shaped stone, suspended from a Cartier necklace, was a gift from Richard Burton to Taylor for her 40th birthday in 1972. With its associations of grand romance and one of Hollywood's most famously tempestuous love affairs, it was an inspired choice for a film about Catherine and Heathcliff. And Robbie's jewelry references didn't end there. At the London premiere, she wore a reproduction of Charlotte Brontë's mourning bracelet, whose original contained hair believed to belong to her sisters Emily and Anne. Clearly, someone had done their literary homework.

Céline Dion has never been one to shy away from a spectacular jewel, but her choices during her triumphant return to the stage in Paris came with more than a little sentiment. For her opening performance, she wore Boucheron's The Address necklace, a black-lacquer-and-diamond creation featuring a 10.01-carat emerald-cut diamond. The connection was deeply personal: her late husband, René Angélil, always wore Boucheron fragrance, and Dion said the necklace made her feel as though he were with her.

Then, in October, Dion revisited a defining moment in her own fashion history. In 1997, she became the first artist to perform twice at a single Oscars ceremony, doing so in a plunging silver Chanel gown by Karl Lagerfeld and a celestial Comète necklace. Nearly three decades later, Matthieu Blazy reimagined the gown for her Paris residency, complete with a new version of the necklace. Inspired by Gabrielle Chanel's original 1932 high-jewelry design, the piece featured 1,080 diamonds totaling more than 67 carats, set in platinum and white gold. Some things really are worth repeating.

Zendaya and longtime stylist Law Roach have made something of a specialty of dressing for the part, and their jewelry choices are no exception. There was the Bulgari Serpenti necklace, complete with a 93.83-carat emerald, at the 2021 Venice premiere of Dune, and the spectacular Chopard diamond bib worn with a sculptural Schiaparelli breastplate for The Odyssey this year. (Let’s not forget those controversial ancient Iranian gold medallion earrings that got people talking.) But perhaps her most intriguing accessory appeared during the Spider-Man: Brand New Day press tour in Shanghai: a diamond-set spider brooch with a yellow sapphire at its center, pinned to an archival Atelier Versace gown. The reference was obvious enough, but the provenance proved rather more complicated when two jewelry houses claimed credit for the jewel. The brooch was eventually traced to David Webb, though precisely how it ended up on Zendaya’s hip remains a mystery. A tangled web, indeed!

Few men have done more for the brooch in recent years than Colman Domingo. At the 2026 Emmys, he pinned Boucheron's Green Garden brooch, an extravagant arrangement of green tourmalines, diamonds, and green lacquer, to the fuchsia sash of his custom Valentino ensemble by Alessandro Michele. The piece comes from Boucheron's Like a Queen collection, inspired by a double-clip brooch given to Princess Elizabeth for her 18th birthday. Domingo's appreciation for jewelry history runs deep: at the 2025 Oscars, he wore a Boucheron ribbon brooch dating to 1956, while his 2025 Met Gala look featured the house's dramatic rock-crystal-and-diamond Iceberg necklace. Evidently, he sees no reason to leave the family jewels to the ladies.

Zoë Kravitz has a particular talent for making extraordinary jewelry look like something she just threw on. Case in point: the 20-carat Jessica McCormack diamond pendant she wore on a simple black cord for an appearance on Late Night with Seth Meyers last summer, paired with a cropped Saint Laurent vest, low-slung pinstripe trousers, and a bandana. As the jeweler's first-ever ambassador, Kravitz has made a convincing case for wearing serious diamonds with decidedly casual ease. At the 2026 Met Gala, she took a more surrealist approach, pairing her black lace Saint Laurent gown with McCormack's bespoke Medallion Cry Baby earrings and matching ring. Inspired by the imagery of Man Ray and Salvador Dalí, the earrings featured diamond tears suspended from golden eyes.

Leave it to Cole Escola to turn a piece of antique jewelry into a theatrical history lesson. At the 2025 Tony Awards, the Oh, Mary! playwright and star wore a custom ice-blue Wiederhoeft gown inspired by the costume Bernadette Peters wore to accept her Tony for Annie Get Your Gun in 1999. But the real deep cut was around Escola's neck: an antique pendant containing a portrait of Laura Keene, the actress and theater manager who was starring in Our American Cousin at Ford's Theatre on the night Abraham Lincoln was assassinated. The reference was particularly apt for the creator of a comedy about Mary Todd Lincoln, and hardly a casual choice. Escola has even spoken of visiting Keene's grave since Oh, Mary! opened.

Chase Sui Wonders has developed a fondness for Tiffany & Co.'s feathered friends. At the 2026 Venice Film Festival, she wore Jean Schlumberger's iconic Bird on a Rock brooch, featuring a diamond of more than 13 carats and a pink sapphire, pinned to a simple ribbon around her neck. It was an inventive way to wear a design that dates back to 1965, and considerably more interesting than an ordinary diamond necklace. At the Actor Awards earlier in the year, she had opted for another interpretation of the house's avian motif: a Bird on a Rock necklace set with a 12-carat rubellite, accompanied by diamond-and-rubellite earrings totaling more than 33 carats.

#6623. We Come to Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter Live at Carnegie Hall to Feel

The film, shot in 35mm, is currently “on tour” at movie theaters around the country

The Cambridge Dictionary recently announced that its selection for Word of the Year is human. Human as an adjective that denotes that something was not made by computers or A.I. (Last year’s word was parasocial.) The editor at Cambridge told the Times that they found phrases like “human governance,” “human written,” and “human need” come up often in their research.

I think about this while I’m at the movie theater watching Paul Thomas Anderson’s latest film, Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, which documents the 23-year-old’s performance at the legendary venue. It is the film’s release date, and all of the showings are sold out, but since I’ve come alone, I am able to find the perfect seat. Winter’s face is large on the screen, and it’s almost expressionless except for his eyebrows, barely peeking out from underneath what can truly only be called a mop of hair, which curves this way and that way as the only proof of the emotional energy he is exerting. Otherwise, he seems to simply open his mouth and the words come out, devastating and romantic, because what else would they do? What else would he do but this? For an hour and a half, we all sit here enthralled by a single man and a piano. Then I think about how my most recent moviegoing experiences required staring at people talking, or thinking, or simply staring at a very close range. (I’d just seen You Can See Everything a few weeks before.) We come to the movies to see humans was my brain-rot thought, in the style of Nicole Kidman’s famous AMC commercial. (Brain rot was Oxford’s 2024 Word of the Year.)

I think back to when it all began. The day after Valentine’s Day last year, my friend Tran casually texted me, asking, “You get into this guy?” with a Spotify link to an album called Heavy Metal by someone called Cameron Winter. I couldn’t tell what it would sound like just by looking at the cover, which was a close-up of his face, criss-crossed by silver chains, but what I soon found were songs dominated by a deep baritone voice and a sweet, jangly guitar or a kind of hazily sensual piano. Who was this guy? Well, it turned out he was the lead singer of this band called Geese—not to be confused with Goose—which he’d started when he was a teen with his high school friends. He’d made this album (jokingly rumored to have been recorded in Guitar Centers, from which he was now banned) and released it without any fanfare that previous December, against the advice of people who knew him and thought the record was too strange or would somehow interfere with the planned Geese release in the new year. (That album, Getting Killed, was released in September 2025 and turned the band from little-known Brooklyn musicians into both “saviors of rock & roll” and “music label psy-ops,” topping off numerous best-of lists and garnering multiple Grammy nominations.) But none of that had happened yet.

As I sat in the movie theater, I wondered how many of us in the audience had also been at the performance. What were we looking for in a recording of something we had experienced firsthand? That night, Winter emerged on stage and sat at the piano, his back turned to us. We watched his head sink beneath his shoulders as if he was searching for something deeper inside the instrument, or maybe he was becoming one with it. We had no choice but to completely give ourselves to the music. But Anderson’s camera was nimble and dug itself in other places: a peephole on the stage that looked out to Winter in the foreground and the ocean of people behind him, indeed turning the whole affair into a kind of landscape, swooping in from the audience to Winter at the piano like a detective looking for the culprit of an unnamed crime, or training his lens on the oversize shadow cast by Winter over the audience sitting stage left. I think, “Oh, this is like a musical Rashomon.”

During “Drinking Age,” as he sings, “Today, I met who I’m gonna be / from now on / and he’s a piece of shit,” the screen goes dark blue, with only his faint silhouette visible, the weight of his words carrying a brief silence so that you sit there in the emotion. Other times, we experience through Anderson’s POV, seeing the ushers open the backstage doors so that he can step onstage, deftly twirling the camera around Winter’s body. This time he is singing “$0.” It’s perhaps the best song on the album (or at least according to this writer), where he sings with wild abandon, “God is real / God is real / I’m not kidding, God is actually real I’m not kidding this time / I think God is actually for real …” Anderson trains his camera on one of the dramatic light fixtures at the concert hall, a round disc that resembles the sun, then he pans to the audience, then to Winter, small on stage, confessing his small miracle. Afterward, as if exhausted, he delicately plays a simple riff on the piano, while there’s a close-up of his face on screen with heavenly rays of light reflected on his face. I believed him when I first heard it on the album, and I believed him twice more as I heard him sing it live.

Winter stands up; the show is over. The lights come up, and the crowd rises to its feet. I can’t remember now if there was an encore, though I do remember we stood there applauding for a very long time, emotionally drained but joyful that we’d been witnesses. On the screen, the credits roll over images of the crowd, and the two teen girls sitting to my right have spotted themselves in the audience, elated. Winter comes back out for two more songs.

The movie ends. “Cameron Winter. Live at Carnegie Hall. Dead at 23,” flashes on the screen. Inside the movie theater, the people applaud. I’m still thinking of Winter singing of “com[ing] down to see / my private ceremonies / All on the floor of this room,” and I think, yes, we’re all here in ceremony—or are we in communion?—with one another. The human need for human connection, for human revelations.

#6622. Bella Hadid Just Wants to Settle Down in a Small Town With “a Man That I Love” and Have “Lots of Children”

The supermodel gets honest about her goals for the future in her new cover story for Harper’s Bazaar

Bella Hadid may be the face of Saint Laurent and Prada, and she may own every high-profile runway she’s on, but her long-term life goal doesn’t involve spotlights or mega fame. In her new cover story for Harper’s Bazaar, the supermodel opens up like never before about what she sees for her future.

“From an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion shows you do. And that is really important in our industry, especially when you’re building,” she notes. “But for me, I am different.”

While she feels endlessly lucky for her place in the fashion industry, and admits that having opened the Victoria’s Secret fashion show last month was a dream come true, she yearns for an easy life surrounded by family and nature.

“Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals,” Hadid says.

A cowgirl at heart, the Orebella founder has down-to-earth goals that do not necessarily involve modeling, but do involve having a small local business, leaning into hobbies that bring her peace, and becoming a wife and mother.

“I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community. I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother,” she says. “It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me. My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it.”

#6621. As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

This morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release. It’s the first new installment of the franchise since 2013; the one whose first trailer was released three years ago; the one that probably cost over a billion dollars to produce; the one set in a satirical, fictionalized south Florida; the one described in this very magazine as “the peak of entertainment.” During my first four hours with the game, I made a few hundred dollars doing odd jobs, performed several repairs on my swamp-front fixer-upper, knocked out a few sets of kettlebell swings on the deck, did favors for two friendly neighbors, and ran a mile to retrieve a freshly repainted car I left behind at a fishing spot just outside of town. I’m writing in vague terms not only to avoid spoiling the game’s plot but because, so far, it hasn’t been all that exciting. The absurd and hyperrealistic mundanity of its gameplay is, simply, astonishing, and more than I ever could have wanted from a franchise I’ve been playing for nearly a quarter of a century.

Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child. I wasn’t even aware of their existence until learning of the franchise’s third entry, and the first in 3D. I discovered GTA in a hotel room in Wichita Falls, TX, a small city just a stone’s throw from Oklahoma, because a classmate named Zach (or Zack) risked damaging his PS2 by toting it along on a school trip. We were there for the annual Texas Thespian Festival, an opportunity for dramatically inclined teenagers to perform plays and musicals in front of strange kids from strange schools and compete for prizes that, like most awards, quickly lost meaning after they were bestowed. After attending the required main stage productions, many of which were watered down to their school-friendly “Junior” adaptations—Into the Woods without the second act deaths and darkness, Guys & Dolls with considerably less gambling—we returned to the nearby hotel where students slept three to a room and were told to behave. For several nights we took turns playing this impossibly violent and vulgar game, five or six of us huddled around the television parked on a dresser no one used. We stole cars, killed non-player characters with assault rifles, and even completed an occasional story mission, most of which required, well, stealing cars and killing non-player characters with assault rifles. We were actors, and wasn’t gaming just another form of performance?

I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity. Before that moment, he was simply an intimidatingly charming and friendly older boy I knew best for playing Romeo in a production that our school’s theater director chose to set during the Vietnam War for reasons he was unable to articulate. (In that, my first stage role, I was cast as Juliet’s unnamed little brother, a role that doesn’t exist in the original text.) Of course I’d played video games before that weekend—Myst, Rollercoaster Tycoon and a Titanic-themed mystery were my favorites at that point—but never before had I experienced something so immersive or graphically impressive. It was loud and exciting, a simulation of real life at its most extreme and chaotic. When I got home, I knew the console–and GTA 3–had to be mine. My life, laser-focused on math homework and our theater director’s post-apocalyptic interpretation of Antigone, could have really used a thrill.

I traded in my PlayStation, a Christmas gift from years earlier on which I played mostly rented or borrowed adventure games, and used money I’d saved from mowing lawns (my family’s own, and those of a few elderly neighbors), to pay the balance. The only game I wanted was GTA III, and it’s the only one I played for months. The novelty was the thing. There was a story, of course: some nameless protagonist with a chiseled, low-polygon face committing crimes and various acts of violence to achieve a goal of… staying alive? Perhaps that’s the goal of most games, maybe even the goal of life itself. I skipped cutscenes in favor of driving from one glowing cylindrical marker to the next, shooting police officers in the head and picking up sex workers who did unseen, noisy things to my character that made the stolen cars bounce up and down like a lowrider with hydraulics. I’d largely missed the groundbreaking graphics of the N64 era—having never played Zelda or Mario Kart or GoldenEye outside the bedrooms of childhood friends with bigger houses and never-ending supplies of soda in the fridge—which meant my first truly passionate dive into console gaming was filled with manic, gratuitous violence. The original PlayStation was for catching troublemaking monkeys in nets and flying around gentle landscapes as a purple dragon. The PS2, though, was for imagining a life of crime. That my parents allowed me to play these games at all still surprises me, but I suppose to them anything was better than me getting drunk at parties I knew were happening but was never invited to.

By the time Grand Theft Auto: Vice City was released the following year, I had a part time job at a local AMC, so I bought the game with money earned selling popcorn and cleaning that same popcorn off the floor. Playing it was a reward for completing an essay on Ernest Hemingway or telling multiple moviegoers that we couldn’t give refunds simply because they “didn’t like” Men In Black 2. The game’s soundtrack introduced me to songs that still activate memories sitting cross-legged on the carpet of my bedroom, turning the volume down as low as I could to prevent my father from stepping inside and saying, gravely, “Am I going to have to turn that off?” To this day, I can’t hear Laura Branagin’s “Self Control” without conjuring Tommy Vercetti, the protagonist of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, driving a motorcycle down a sparsely populated road flanked by neon-lit palm trees. For months, I listened to more in-game radio than the local Top 40 station, unaware at the time that its curated period playlists would shape my musical appetite for the rest of my life.

The third installment of that PS2 trilogy, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, came out two years later, when I was a freshman in college. I was 18, adjusting to life in a new city, and trying desperately to make friends. The game was less a reward for hard work than a balm when I didn’t feel like socializing, a distraction from my countless first semester anxieties. By the time I completed its main story, life away from home had become normal. I had new friends, new obligations, new problems. I used my PS2 as a DVD player almost exclusively, watching several movies a week, all borrowed from Netflix (during its original red-envelope form) and the school library. By the time GTA 4 was released, I’d lost interest in gaming altogether. We were in a recession, and I was hellbent on keeping my very first real job. In fact, I didn’t play another Grand Theft Auto game until 2013, on a PS3 Slim (the console’s discounted, late-generation entry), weeks after my now-husband and I moved into our first apartment together. In the time since my last GTA experience, I’d come out of the closet, moved across the country, started a new career, adopted my first cat, and made an entirely new group of close friends. A franchise that was once a distraction from teenage malaise was now pure, unadulterated fun. Gone were the days of playing it at a low volume–I turned it all the way up, and didn’t skip cut scenes. I was there for the story as well as the spectacle.

13 years later, the longest ever interval between new installments, my relationship with gaming has evolved alongside the games themselves. It’s not enough to be distracted; being distracted is now our default state. Disturbances arise, whether seeking them or not: a text message in the middle of a terrible Peacock show; a news alert regarding a global calamity about which you can do nothing but panic; the jittering beeps of FaceTime call while reading a wonderful novel, or that mindless, habitual scroll through a feed that shows videos meant to be seen but not remembered. Lately I’ve turned to gaming for total immersion, for sensations of genuine awe that might keep me from succumbing to the dopamine rush of my phone. I spent much of the summer replaying Kingdom Come Deliverance and its sequel, a pair of life simulators set in medieval Europe. In those games, every action has a consequence, and every success is hard-fought and requires patience.

After several hours in its impossibly dense world, GTA 6 seems to be encouraging a similar sense of duty. My real life is fine, often even good. It’s the kind of life I thought impossible when the franchise first entered my life nearly a quarter century ago. I’m not bowled over by the game because it’s better or even more fun than the life I live outside Vice City—there are gun-toting mass murderers in both, after all—but because it’s totally different. Even when you’re comfortable in your own life, isn’t it extraordinary to enter another? The games have always been about adults, and for adults. It says so right on the box. Since 2002, their goals have fundamentally remained the same: get a job, make money, stay alive. As a teenager, its simulated depravity was funny and exciting, with graphics and gameplay so vivid I could feel like a kid again. But now, at 40? With 20-plus years of GTA under my belt and a life 16-year-old me would find more unbelievable than the functionalities of the PS5 Pro? No game has ever made me feel older. What a privilege that is.

#6620. Chain-Strap Bags Are Back in the Spotlight—The Best to Invest In

When you think of chain-strap handbags, an elegant nighttime bag likely comes to mind. But while the look has long been synonymous with dressed-up occasions, there’s no reason to reserve them for after-dark outings.

When Gabrielle Chanel introduced her now-iconic 2.55 handbag in February 1955 (hence the name), she designed it to free women from having to hand-carry their purses. More than 70 years later, the quilted shoulder bag and its signature chain remain among the most recognizable handbags in fashion history.

The chain bag has come a long way since then. Today’s iterations extend beyond classic flap bags and dainty evening clutches, encompassing everything from slouchy leather shoulder bags and and roomy bucket shapes to structured top-handle bags and quilted crossbody purses. The materials are just as varied: leather and suede offer everyday appeal, while satin, velvet, and embellished finishes keep it in evening bag territory. Even the gold and silver hardware has evolved, with chunky, sculptural links making just as much of a statement as delicate straps.

The resurgence began with the spring/summer 2026 collections, when designers including Chloé, Ferragamo, and Valentino brought chain-strap bags back into the spotlight. By fall/winter 2026, Chanel, Dior, and Gabriela Hearst were putting their own spin on the trend, experimenting with new proportions, textures, and metal chain handles. Some incorporated oversized links into otherwise minimalist silhouettes, while others treated chunky chain handles as decorative elements that could double as jewelry.

When shopping for a chain bag, consider the weight and construction of the hardware, especially if you plan to carry yours every day or to work. Look for chains that feel substantial and luxe without being unnecessarily heavy. Pay attention to how the strap sits on your shoulder, too; a leather shoulder insert or leather-interwoven chain can help prevent metal links from digging in when the bag is full. Convertible chains (or removable straps) allow you to switch between shoulder and crossbody wear, making the chain crossbody bag all the more practical and versatile.

Whether you’re looking for an everyday workhorse with a hint of shine or a statement-making finishing touch for your next night out, there’s a style to suit every occasion. Ahead, discover the best chain strap bags to shop now, from timeless designer icons to fresh interpretations of the enduring silhouette.

#6619. Bella Hadid Opens Up About Being Rejected From the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show

Bella Hadid has become one of the biggest supermodels in the world, and this year, she even opened the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show—a runway on which she has become a regular. However, her success is the result of a lot of work, and many rejections.

In her December 2026/January 2027 cover story for Harper’s Bazaar, Hadid opens up about a time, over a decade ago, when she was rejected after auditioning for the VS show. In a conversation with Bazaar’s editor in chief, Samira Nasr, Hadid is asked how it felt to come full circle. Nasr recalls: “On one of our first shoots together, you were really upset because you didn’t get the Victoria’s Secret show. And I said to you, ‘One day, they will be begging you to be in their show.’ And I could tell you didn’t believe me. Your whole body shut down. And three days ago, you opened Victoria’s Secret. Holy shit.”

Hadid admits that she often feels like she’s in a daydream. “I still don’t believe you, to be honest,” the Orebella founder says to Nasr. “I feel like people are just AI-ing me onto the runway. I think that it’s so crazy how time passes and you still have some kind of impostor syndrome.”

She goes on to add: “No matter how hard you work, there’s always another girl who is more deserving, more beautiful, and has worked so hard to be able to get that spot. Ten years ago, I remember that moment too, where I never thought I would get the show, but I think that God always has a plan, and I truly believe at that time I wasn’t ready. I don’t think I’ve been ready until this year, to be honest. In past years, I was going to my horse-show finals in the morning, flying straight to the Victoria’s Secret show that day, doing rehearsal right before, and then pulling what we call a Bella, and Belinda comes out, and we just act. But this year, I felt really strong.”

Over the years, Hadid has opened up about turning to an alter ego, named Belinda, to handle the pressures of her career. However, when Nasr asks if she feels like it was her or Belinda walking the Victoria’s Secret runway this time, Hadid responds: “You know what? Fortunately and unfortunately, I think it was Bella this year.”

#6618. This Piping Hot Zenith Collaboration Explains the Future of the Watch Market

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

In early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November. The latest Zenith G.F.J., made in partnership with the Los Angeles-based independent watchmaker J.N. Shapiro, is a gorgeous timepiece that combines the former’s mechanical know-how with Shapiro’s meticulously handmade dials. Over four months before the watch was even unveiled to the public, Marietta shared that 20 of the 25 pieces produced had already been sold. Of all the releases from the major Swiss brands in 2026, none better represent the future of luxury watchmaking than this high-end, fussily made, independent-adjacent, sold-out-before-you-ever-heard-about-it G.F.J.

Zenith recently announced that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market. “All of us in our segment, which is described as mid-range, are going through a very difficult period,” Zenith CEO Benoit De Clerck told staff as he explained the restructuring, according to Le Temps. The brand has been shifting upmarket since last year, when it released a rainbow gem-set version of its flagship sport watch. The G.F.J. is the cornerstone of that new business. As the economy tilts even further in favor of the uber-rich, it’s also altering where the bulk of the profits come from for watchmakers. “Wealthy people are still wealthy, and even more wealthy,” Marietta said. “It’s easier [now] to sell high-end watches than watches for 3,000 to 5,000 Swiss francs.”

That’s true. Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Company, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year. Not for the brand’s flagship Chronomaster, which remains firmly in the starter luxury watch zone at $12,300, but for the far more expensive G.F.J., which starts at $49,900. “The luxury direction is the game changer,” Monroy said. Feldmar only received three G.F.J.s to allocate in 2026 and they were all quickly snapped up. There’s now a waitlist building at the retailer for the upscale model.

When it comes to the G.F.J., Zenith has acted like MacGyver, finding endless uses for its smash-hit model. First released in the spring of 2025, the watch received two very pretty, well-received sequels earlier this year. In March, I got to test out the new onyx-dial version for just a few hours before I had to send it along to Hollywood stylist Fabio Immediato, who promptly strapped it on Simu Liu’s wrist for the Oscars.

Over the summer, Zenith also launched this double-signed program, which allows the brand to work with independent makers like J.N. Shapiro. Before this latest release, the Swiss brand linked up with Japan’s beloved Naoya Hida.

That watch was a fascinating representation of the project—the spotlessly clean dial was straight out of the latter’s workshop. Zenith, a historic brand backed by LVMH, ceded control entirely to the small Japanese indie. It was a massive success. To allocate the pieces, Marietta said they narrowed the list to 10 clients, mainly from the Naoya Hida side, then sent an email that included the price tag of 60,000 Swiss francs but zero images of the watch. “They said yes right away, trusting us with the design,” Marietta said. “And that’s a great testimony of how the trust can be at that level when you buy a piece for [$75,000] without even seeing it, not even a picture.”

In the topsy-turvy world of watches in 2026, it’s much sexier to be an independent brand than one in the stable of the world’s largest luxury conglomerate. Marietta calls the G.F.J. “an independent brand within our global lineup,” pointing to the high-level finishing and historic movement inside the piece—the type of nerdy details that appeal to the most seasoned collectors driving the industry. “The G.F.J. collection itself is bringing us new clients,” Marietta said. “It's attracting clients who did not really have Zenith on their radar. These guys were more A. Lange & Söhne clients or with independents.”

Zenith created irresistible bait for this new stripe of collectors. The new J.N. Shapiro-designed G.F.J. is absolutely gorgeous. The partners leverage the LA independent’s dedication to creating its dials by hand through a technique known as engine turning. I got to visit Shapiro’s workshop a few years ago and was charmed by the contrast of the brand’s cavernous industrial warehouse and the row of almost medieval-looking engine-turning machines lined up at the front of the room.

The dials of the new collaborative watches were painstakingly made on those very machines—on which a single mistake means tossing the whole thing in the bin—and then shipped off to Switzerland, where Zenith watchmakers installed them into cases. There are three different patterns on the dial, including a basketweave at the center and Shapiro’s signature invention, the Infinity Weave, inside the subdial. Much like on the Naoya Hida version, the dial is all Shapiro. Marietta notes, however, that it already resembles the brick pattern seen on the original G.F.J., which is based on the exterior of Zenith’s manufacture in Le Locle.

Zenith plans to release two collaborative versions of the G.F.J. annually moving forward. According to Marietta, a couple of years down the road, the brand may allow their indie partners to go beyond the dial and play with the case and movement as well.

With the G.F.J., Zenith has created something that is tailor-made for today’s collectors. Seven-figure pieces are currently booming at auction, and it would take Moses himself to part the money flooding into the market right now. These deep-pocketed collectors are most interested in watches from independent makers: Auction houses have sold more million-dollar F.P. Journe watches this year than they have from either Rolex or Patek Philippe. As collectors search for the next hot watchmaker, they’re finding exactly what they’re looking for in a 161-year-old Swiss luxury brand.

#6617. 27 Luxurious (and Truly Over-the-Top) Beauty and Wellness Gifts

Some people are fans of practical gifts. Others want an experience, like a beach getaway or ski trip. One of my favorite gifts to receive? The ability to be a voyeur into your holiday season.

I live for social media posts of ornament-laden trees sparkling over piles of color-coordinated packages or perfectly curated table settings. Ditto Instagram stories featuring people unwrapping presents with nary a care for their delicate camellia bows or designer ribbons. (“Save them!” I silently scream, proving my grandmother is still with me in spirit.) Every time a holiday rolls around, I’m waiting to see what the Kardashians will get up to—matching golf carts for all the kids on Christmas? Hermès china, ultimately returned? A suite of identical puppies? Show me now.

In the off season (aka January to October), I fantasize about what will be next—what are the greatest gifts to give if there were no budget restrictions? Once, I was told there was “no budget” when it came to a shopping experience (and if the person who uttered the phrase to me unwisely assumed I would be at least sensible, no dice)—I applied the same mantra to these beauty and wellness items in this story.

The following gifts are a short and sweet selection of beauty and wellness offerings of Kardashian-level caliber—so fanciful, delightful, extravagant and extreme that any beauty lover will be wowed … along with anybody who is following along on social media, too.

There is, in fact, a gift for your sardine-obsessed, protein-pilled family member. This very cute, very heavy advent calendar from Los Angeles-based Fishwife has everything from their classic Sardines (filled with vitamin D, B12, and omega-3 fatty acids, as well as essential minerals including iodine, selenium, iron, calcium, and potassium, phew!) to an adorable keychain and the collaboration with Bag Balm.

If The Glucose Goddess’s decision to take a hunk of parmesan cheese to Fashion Week inspired anybody in your life to double down on this high-protein, low-lactose cheese, why not give them what I imagine could be … well, at least a few months’ supply? It’s 80 pounds, which means there’s about 13,000 grams of protein inside the rind.

You want to touch grass. You also don’t want to touch grass with your bare feet, because you live in New York. Instead, try a pair of barefoot shoes that are fashion-forward and made of luxurious cashmere.

Poor fruitcake, it’s always the butt of the joke when it comes to holiday sweets. But this one from perennially chic Flamingo Estate will not only wow visually, but perhaps even change people’s tune. Created in collaboration with the actually quite Santa Claus-looking Shannon Swindle, the pastry chef at trendy LA hotspot Funke, there are plenty of fruits in this cake (as the name would imply). But more importantly? It’s soaked in a lot of dark rum.

A collab between Nike and fitness tech company Hyperice, these slides were made to help athletes recover from long days on their feet—and yes, that includes women wearing heels all day, too. There’s a tiny pod inside each slide that warms and vibrates, helping to relax tired muscles, though if you just have chronically cold feet, we imagine these would be nice, too.

Lymphatic drainage was one of 2026’s buzziest beauty trends. This is the gift for the man or woman who has been dry-brushing since Gwyneth Paltrow first uttered the word on Goop. Made in France, the palm-sized lacquered brush (which comes in two shades—aubergine and powder pink) is totally vegan and top-shelf worthy.

This tabletop water purifier removes 80 potential contaminants from your drinking water (like microplastics and PFAS) as well as tracks your daily ounces.

Yes, it sort of looks like that creature from Stranger Things or a pop-art object. But Dyson’s newest air purifier is here to do the lord’s work (especially as the EPA continues to face budget cuts). It can work across multiple rooms (great for those of us who live in a tiny New York apartment), heats and cools, and reports back what’s in the air at any given moment.

Is it sexy to gift an alarm clock? Maybe not. But you know what the sexiest thing of all is? Ditching your phone in another room and getting an incredible night’s sleep. This alarm clock can actually help with those things, along with making waking up easier (it has a two-phase alarm that will gently wake you up, not startle).

Fitness trackers can be ugly, it’s true. But if you’re going to truly commit to wearing it every day (ahem), might as well spruce it up a bit. This cover is made of 14k gold and step-cut diamonds (that’s my favorite kind!), but the Henri Noël team can also do custom orders if sapphires, emeralds, or rubies are more your vibe.

One of the most ubiquitous beauty products in the world is a nail cutter—but that doesn’t mean it has to be basic or utilitarian. Instead, any nail lover will love this gold and monogrammed five-piece kit from Louis Vuitton, which has everything you need to fix a manicure emergency (scissors, tweezers, nail clipper, and nail file) and could probably help you survive if stranded on a desert island, too.

The Sisters of the Valley are Brides of Christ … who love weed. This handmade salve is made with hemp-based CBD that is harvested during the moon cycle (to give it peak potency), along with coconut oil, vitamin E, and calendula. Hail Mary!

Red light therapy is scientifically proven to reduce redness, inflammation, fine lines, and more—and while the face devices are great, why stop there? Instead, work smarter, not harder, with this combo: The Celluma shield mask is lightweight and flexible so you can bend it to cover your face and scalp, while the Bon Charge mask covers you from neck to toes. I like how this combo truly forces you to slow down (try doing TCM meditation or listen to a podcast) for at least 20 minutes a day.

You loved your trip to Fiji. The sensible next step? A fragrance that reminds you of the divine time. The juice inside this frosted glass bottle smells just like a giant arrangement of incredible white flowers—jasmine, white gardenia, and frangipani.

Mrs. Prada’s sustainable spirit has made its way to your lunchbox, too. The stainless steel pail, made in collaboration with Black + Blum, can be divided into two portions, and comes with a set of utensils, so you can eat anywhere with style. Perfect for your bean salad, wheat meat, or retinol-rich diet.

For the beauty lover who is obsessed with logomania—the Hermès lash curler, which has an orange pad so you can go all-in on the brand’s signature shade.

Halle Berry loves her Eight Sleep (even saying that it helped her through menopause), and I do, too. The latest version of the cooling-heating-moving-sleep tracking mattress pad is smaller than ever—perfect for Manhattan apartments—and can help you get a great night’s sleep.

If you’re going to Korea for any type of beauty treatment, a translator is a must-have (especially if you’re interested in doing work on your face!). Jennifer Seo’s team at Aneue Concierge not only books the appointments for you and sends along all the details in a schedule, but they also tag along to make sure you know exactly what you’re getting.

My willpower to stop doomscrolling is more kindergartener who just tried T-ball for the first time, less Olympian. So I’ve outsourced the job for me. Brick is a physical social media blocker that you have to tap to unlock—though I’m thinking about leveling up to the dumb smartphone Wise, which has all the necessities like we did when the phone first came out, none of the brain-sucking frills.

If somebody you know (or you yourself) asks to always see the photos from their colonoscopies, wants to keep pulled teeth, and is really curious about every marker of their health, one of these kits—which measure your skin biome, hormones, or gut sensitivities, respectively—will be a hit.

Taylor Swift used this bra to help keep her posture in place while training for The Eras Tour. It’s a compression-like garment that holds everything from your shoulders to your chest in place, so it keeps you both secure and straight-up.

Functional can be fun (and fab!)—like this caviar-tin-inspired mirror compact, one of Estée Lauder’s limited-edition holiday designs.

For the person in your life who loves to carry multiple drinks. While this fridge may be mini, its perks are mighty: it can hold 77 cans of your favorite sparkling water or healthy soda (or 27 bottles if you’re trying to up your antioxidant intake), is controlled by your iPhone, and can even tell you what’s stocked inside (or if you need to re-up on kombucha while at the grocery store).

I’m constantly searching for a better way to organize all my daily medications (antidepressants! thyroid meds! migraine meds!), along with the handful of supplements I take daily. And while a gum ball machine would be my first choice, I’m on too many medications for that. Why not this solid Calacatta marble pillbox instead?

#6616. The 15 Beauty Products Our Editors Loved in November

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Including Bazaar-approved hair combs and our beauty director’s favorite $10 drugstore find

I’m always asked, “What are your favorite beauty products?”—and honestly, I find that question hard to answer. My role as Bazaar’s beauty director requires me to test hundreds, if not thousands, of launches yearly, so my favorites change daily as I discover what’s new. I’m not alone in this.
