#6615. Why Peptide Skincare Might Actually Be Worth Your While, According to Experts

The recent buzz around peptides came to a head last month when U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced that six unregulated injectables, including the highly controversial “Wolverine stack” BPC-157 and TB-500, will now be available for broad use throughout the United States. Meanwhile, unsurprising to derms and estheticians everywhere, the rising tide of interest in peptides has spilled over into skincare, where the molecules have long served as an active ingredient.

“I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” says Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’

“It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” says Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in New York City. “They’ve been incorporated into cosmetic formulations for decades, with ingredients like matrixyl helping to popularize them in the early 2000s. What’s exciting now is how much more sophisticated the formulations have become.”

If you’re curious about peptide-based skincare products—what they potentially can do, what they definitely cannot—and which products experts recommend for the best results, here’s everything you need to know.

Peptides, regardless of whether they’re injected via syringe or applied topically with a serum or cream, are short chains of amino acids that instruct your body to execute specific functions. Insulin, for example, is a peptide that helps the body regulate blood sugar, and it’s been in use since the 1920s. More recently, GLP-1 drugs (short for glucagon-like peptide-1) have been found to curb food cravings and slow stomach emptying, making them highly effective for weight loss. The list of uses for peptides is virtually endless, ranging from muscle growth and wound healing to balancing hormones and managing inflammation.

In skincare, topical peptides work much the same way as their injectable counterparts, but on a more localized level, directing your skin to carry out specific functions, “the first of which tends to be increasing production of collagen and elastin, which are two of the major determinants of skin quality,” says Dr. Peterson. They’ve also been shown to help even out skin tone, repair the skin barrier, and reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles.

The world of peptides is still a bit of a Wild West. A quick Google search for peptide skincare will yield dozens of results for unresearched compounds promising you flawless skin. And then, of course, there are the influencers. “You see all these kids on TikTok who are talking about their beauty routines, and they’re like 19 years old,” says Peterson. “It’s like, ‘Amazing, your skin obviously looks great, because you’re a child.’” In reality, the list of peptides that you can truly depend on to move the needle (without an actual needle) is surprisingly short, at least until more research is done.

“The two peptides that are out right now that have any sort of viable data on them are palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and GHK-Cu,” says Peterson. Signaling peptides, as they’re called—such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, better known as matrixyl—have some of the strongest clinical and anecdotal evidence for stimulating collagen and reducing the appearance of wrinkles. Although, as Peterson points out, much of the scientific data has been industry funded, “so we always have to be a bit skeptical.”

Carrier peptides—like GHK-Cu, a popular copper peptide—on the other hand, “have some good lab data, but very minimal human data,” Peterson says. Nonetheless, products containing GHK-Cu are widely heralded for their ability to repair damaged tissue, reduce inflammation, and stimulate production of collagen and elastin. “I find copper peptides particularly interesting because of the research surrounding tissue repair and collagen-related remodeling pathways,” says Sloan.

As for acetyl hexapeptide-8, or argireline, as it’s more commonly known—aka “botox in a bottle”—don’t waste your money. “From a physiological perspective, it can’t possibly work,” says Peterson, who explains that the molecules of this particular peptide are simply too large to pass through the surface of the skin. He compares it to skincare products that contain collagen rather than spur the body to produce its own. “Collagen is a massive molecule,” he says. “It would be like putting cow’s milk on your face—it’s not going to do anything.” Sure enough, a 2023 study found the effects of topical argireline to be “not statistically significant.”

Instead, for those looking for the most noticeable results, Sloan recommends seeking out products that combine proven peptides with complementary, similarly validated ingredients—like SkinCeuticals’ P-TIOX Anti-Wrinkle Peptide Cream. “I like that the cream also incorporates ceramides, niacinamide, and moisturizing ingredients, making it an interesting option for someone looking to address both hydration and visible signs of aging,” she says. Peterson’s pick, The Rich Cream from Augustinus Bader, flanks signaling peptides with hyaluronic acid and vitamin E to improve moisture retention and bolster the skin’s protective barrier.

Peptides are a relatively low-maintenance addition to most skin regimens. “One of the reasons I love incorporating peptides into at-home skincare is that they’re generally well tolerated and relatively easy to combine with other ingredients,” says Sloan, who notes that peptides can typically be used alongside other popular actives like vitamin C, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, and retinoids. “I typically recommend incorporating a peptide serum after cleansing and before moisturizer,” she says.

Just keep in mind that peptides alone won’t take the place of a well-rounded skincare regimen. “The best, most robust data still comes from the tried-and-true favorites of all dermatologists—protecting your collagen with consistent sunscreen use, and the best signaling molecule of them all: topical retinoids,” Peterson says.

And, of course, don’t expect overnight results—despite what social media might have you believe. “Peptides are just signals for your skin, not magic in a bottle,” Peterson says. “The few studies that there are show at least three months of consistent usage before results are seen, so stick it out if you want to give it a real try.”

#6611. Connor Storrie Mixes a “Mezcal Mandy”—and Addresses His Controversial Buzzcut—for Vogue’s Now Serving

“Let me slip into something a little more comfortable,” Connor Storrie says in Vogue’s latest Now Serving episode, trading his Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello ribbed beige V-neck sweater and belted gray trousers—he deadpans it’s his “Sunday walking around the house look”—for a gleaming gold metallic trench coat and aviator sunglasses. (Storrie eventually switches back to cook, though the energy remains decidedly high-fashion.)

First up, the Heated Rivalry actor—and Vogue’s 2026 Best Dressed cover star—prepares his go-to order on a night out: a “Mezcal Mandy.” Skipping the jigger in favor of an eyeball pour of roughly two shots of mezcal over ice, topped with lime and soda water, Storrie takes a sip—despite the shoot taking place at 10 a.m. “This drink says that I don’t want any sugar in my system, but I want a little funk,” he explains.

From there, Storrie moves on to his everyday high-protein staple: a deconstructed burger. Acknowledging that his ingredient list is so minimal that the producers asked him to chop an onion just to get extra knife footage, Storrie karate-chops a pound of ground beef into portions with his bare hands (“So that I don’t get salmonella comments or whatever, I’m going to wash my hands for you people,” he quips) and cooks the patties in grass-fed butter, before topping it with provolone, arugula, thick slices of beefsteak tomato, and a generous squeeze of Dijon mustard. (Another pro tip: he saves the leftover pan grease to cook his six morning eggs the next day.)

Between flipping patties, Storrie reflects on his style evolution, from growing up in Odessa, Texas (“a lot of long cargo shorts, really messed-up tennis shoes, band tees”) and moving to California during the 2016 drop-crotch jogger era, to sitting front row alongside Madonna and Kate Moss at Saint Laurent. He also addresses the internet’s reaction to his recent buzzcut. "I feel like every six months, I’m a completely different person, and I try to honor that,” he says. ‘I like the hair, but people were pissed off. People were not happy. Whatever, screw it. I’m doing my thing.”

While Now Serving guests typically pull out all the stops to impress the crew, Storrie notes that no one is rushing to sample his ultra-minimalist spread. “I don’t care. I like it,” he says with a shrug, before happily polishing off the plate himself. (His next stop? A workout, of course.)

#6610. Exclusive: Shohei Ohtani Just Signed a Historic Deal With New Balance

Shohei Ohtani is used to making history. In addition to his four MLB MVP awards and two World Series rings, the Los Angeles Dodgers two-way great is the first member of the 50/50 club (having racked up 54 home runs and 59 stolen bases during the 2024 season), became the first player to hit three homers and record 10 strikeouts in a single game (which he managed in a 2025 NLCS contest against the Brewers), and earlier this year maintained simultaneous streaks in games on base (48) and innings without an earned run (32 and two-thirds).

Now, the 32-year-old Japanese icon is adding to those accolades with a pioneering endorsement deal, officially extending his relationship with his longtime partner New Balance through to the end of his baseball career. (While a rarefied group of athletes have signed lifetime sponsorship deals—including LeBron James and Cristiano Ronaldo at Nike, and Damian Lillard at Adidas—Ohtani’s new contract appears to be both the first to exclusively cover a star’s playing days and the first of its kind in MLB.)

“There’s a lot of trust,” Ohtani tells me through an interpreter during a sit-down in Boston of his decision to commit to the New England sportswear stalwart for the long haul. “We’ve obviously built friendships, as well. They’ve been able to accommodate my requests, the things I’ve asked for, and, like I said, that takes the involvement of a lot of trust. That relationship has been very, very good and smooth. I had no reservations about extending our relationship.”

Earlier in the day, I shadowed Ohtani at New Balance’s headquarters, where, as part of the agreement, the company is renaming its on-site think tank as the Shohei Ohtani Sports Research Lab. A team of specialists led the Dodgers superstar through a slew of shoes—including his on-field Ohtani 1 model, which will receive new editions in 2027—and then a rack of branded apparel. All of it falls under his Shohei Ohtani Signature Collection, which New Balance launched in 2024 (about a year and a half after the athlete first signed with the company). The collection has grown deliberately and unhurriedly ever since—mirroring his patience in the batter’s box; Ohtani is methodical when it comes to product development and uninterested in rolling out rushed goods with his name slapped on them.

While conducting a kind of footwear postmortem on his 2026 season—which started well, but ended with a rare slump (and left knee and right biceps injuries that kept him from pitching after July 3)—Ohtani noted there’d been some moments of slippage on the heel of his landing foot when pitching. On a printed-out diagram, he used a pencil to sketch ways in which the shoe’s spikes might be slightly reconfigured to find a sweet spot for stability on the mound and speed around the bases. The question of switching footwear between pitching and batting comes up, but Ohtani has not yet done this (and it seems the consensus is to stick with one shoe only).

“I have a lot of direct input into the footwear and apparel,” Ohtani says. “That includes my style, which I like to keep simple, as well as performance-based requests, [like with my] spikes. Some years we make minor changes, and sometimes we’ll make a big change. They understand what I want.”

Ohtani’s apparel line runs across three categories: performance, lifestyle, and fanwear. His custom logo—a striking ink drawing of his figure, designed by the Japanese manga artist Takehiko Inoue—is featured subtly on the bulk of the lineup. “Shohei doesn’t see himself as a glamorous player,” Chris Davis, New Balance brand president and chief marketing officer, tells me. “He sees himself as a gritty, hardworking athlete who wants to get better every day, and his logo reflects this—it has this kind of quiet intensity.”

While some of the future apparel designs boast cool technical features—like detachable, two-in-one, and reversible elements inspired by Ohtani’s two-way play—the man himself is only concerned that his products “fit comfortably and to be easy to wear.” When asked if there’s anyone whose style he likes or is influenced by, Ohtani shrugs. “Honestly, not really. I just like to wear what I like to wear.”

“[Shohei] is very quick and clear with his input,” says Masahiro Uchida, New Balance’s general manager of athlete signature product, who has worked alongside Ohtani for years. “On the performance side, he always prefers softness and a soft hand feel. For the lifestyle side, he prefers clean and simple. He also understands the occasion. He always asks us, ‘Where would I wear this?’” One major goal for Ohtani with his apparel, Uchida adds, is to “support the expansion of baseball culture and show his respect for its heritage. He is a super geek about MLB. He knows so much.”

At 32, the duration of Ohtani’s career—and, now, his New Balance deal—remains an open question. That age can be considered as getting toward the older end in pro baseball, but elite pitchers have a habit of playing well into their 40s—Justin Verlander, for example, just pitched his final season at 43.

Ohtani still plans on being a full two-way player in 2027, with hopes for a Cy Young Award—MLB’s top pitching honor, one of the few laurels he has yet to win—still alive. When the Dodgers’ season ended on October 15, Ohtani told the press that he was “not quite satisfied with how things shaped up on the pitching side.”

What words of advice or motivation does he have, I ask, for the legion of kids hoping to follow in his footsteps? His answer feels like something he might be saying to himself as the next season approaches.

“If you want to become successful, baseball is a sport that takes a lot of repetitive practice,” he says. “You always have to work on your fundamentals. Once you reach a certain level, the sport becomes very, very hard. At that point, you need to remember why you’re playing. Are you playing because you love the sport? If you have that drive, that love for it, then even when it’s tough, you can overcome it.”

If you’re searching for a sneaker that can take you from the office to the gym, On’s Cloudsurfer, which is more than $50 off, is a good candidate. This versatile pair can be used on the treadmill, for road running, and for walking.

#6608. The Best Bridal Shops in NYC to Find Your Dream Wedding Dress

From multi-brand salons to designer showrooms, the best bridal shops in NYC are worth making appointments at to find every piece of your wedding wardrobe.

Whether you live in the U.S. or beyond, New York City is the premier destination to shop for a wedding dress. The best bridal shops in NYC run the gamut from singular showrooms for locally based ateliers, flagship stores for international brands, and salons featuring curated selections from a number of top bridal designers. To-be-weds looking for their own wedding wardrobe can always benefit from a trip to multiple bridal shops around New York to help them discover some of the most beautifully made and innovative designs in the bridal industry.

As a New York local who tried over 100 dresses ahead of her own wedding, wore five looks over her wedding weekend, and regularly attends bridal fashion week both in New York and Barcelona, I am constantly asked where to shop in the city. I myself went to 15 different salons over the course of my search for the perfect wardrobe (and had repeat visits at multiple). While I always advise brides to do a little research to understand the styles they like and what brands they are drawn to, I usually give the same advice. First, try out one or two multi-brand salons with styles within your budget that carry designers you are interested in. This can give you an opportunity to try multiple silhouettes and see options from a variety of designers’ perspectives. Then, choose a few individual brand salons and showrooms to visit.

It’s important to take into consideration that many stores require an appointment fee—and that those can book out months in advance. Also, some stores might offer trunk shows showcasing larger, new collections from certain designers seasonally. So you should invest your time and money strategically into the shops that align with your style and will have the selection you are interested in. However, don’t be afraid to try something different—often, brides fall in love with a wedding dress they never expected.

Ready to start your wedding shopping journey? Ahead—and in no particular order—see our selection of the best bridal shops in NYC.

Mark Ingram Bridal Atelier is often the first stop we would recommend for a bride seeking a wedding gown. You can start your journey trying a wide range of silhouettes from legacy luxury designers and up-and-coming fashion-forward brands. Store owner Mark Ingram is a designer himself, and carries his own brand with classic-leaning silhouettes in store. Those looking for a party dress can also find shorter silhouettes in stock at the Midtown bridal salon.

Designers in Stock: Mira Zwillinger, Dana Harel, Elie Saab, Elly Sofocli, Naeem Khan, Lela Rose, Ines Di Santo, Marmar Halim, Valentini, Mark Ingram Bride, and Vera Wang Haute.

Appointment Fee: Complimentary for a standard appointment. Room services are available starting at $450, which include additional guests, extended appointment times, and beverage service.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

For brides with a slightly more bohemian sensibility, give Spina Bride a try. The luxury bridal salon carries chic designers with a dreamier flair that aren’t often found in most major cities. With a mix of avant-garde and more traditional finds, we often advise this Chelsea salon as a must-stop location when taking a trip to NYC for dress shopping. The multi-boutique salon has also recently partnered with bridal brand Lihi Hod, which opened its flagship on the ground floor. Appointments must be made separately to explore the brand’s selection.

Designers in Stock: Lihi Hod, Floure Studio, J. Andreatta, Yellow by Sahar, Ferrah, Francesca Miranda, Santos Costura, Costarellos, A La Robe, and Chana Marelus.

Appointment Fee: $100 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Spina recommends two independent tailors for off-site alterations.

Located in Tribeca, Jaxon James has a light-filled space ready for a relaxed, personalized shopping experience. Many designers in this salon have styles that lean towards lace, embellishments, and dramatic silhouettes. A large collection of bridal minis also offers the chance to find flirty party looks.

Designers in Stock: Eden Aharon, Maison Margot, Netta Benshabu, Noy Eliyahu, Pallas Couture Privée, Zuleyha Kuru, House of Savin, Jane Hill, Alyne, Rivini, Mariana Hardwick, and Angel Rivera.

Appointment Fee: $50 for a standard appointment and $100 for exclusive trunk shows. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Jaxon James recommends independent tailors for off-site alterations.

If you have ever watched Say Yes to the Dress, you are well aware of Kleinfeld. But don’t worry… a visit doesn’t mean your appointment will be seen on TV. The famous bridal salon offers appointments to thousands of brides annually who come for the wide range of designers in their store. Stylists will pull options for you based on intake forms before your appointment, and you can also browse designers currently showcased on the floor. Many plus-size brides choose to start their journey at Kleinfeld as it has the largest selection of designer silhouettes in expanded sizing to try in the city. There is also a Generation Tux store within the space for grooms looking for their ensembles.

Designers in Stock: Reem Acra, Viktor & Rolf, Ines Di Santo, Sareh Nouri, Peter Langner, Tony Ward, Pnina Tornai, Lee Petra Grebenau, Enaura, Jaclyn Whyte, Anne Barge, Rita Vinieris, Alyne, Netta BenShabu, Esé Azénabor, Maison Signore, Nicole + Felicia, Savannah Miller, Idan Cohen, Alon Livné,, Justin Alexander Signature, Pronovias, Nadia Manjarrez, Hayley Paige, and more.

Appointment Fee: $50 for standard appointments Wednesday through Friday, $125 for Saturday appointments, and $75 for Sunday appointments. VIP appointments begin at $250. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

The NYC outpost of Lovely Bride is a favorite as it provides an elevated experience for clients while offering gowns at more accessible price points. The curation is extensive as well, with options for those seeking traditional gowns, minimal silhouettes, vintage-inspired designs, and contemporary creations.

Designers in Stock: Newhite, Katherine Tash, Saint, Dany Tabet, Renhue, Rue De Seine, Moira Hughes, MWL, Vagabond, Louvienne, Alyssa Kristin, Georgia Young, Savannah Miller, Seraphine, Divine Atelier, and La Premiere.

Appointment Fee: $50 for a standard appointment with four guests and $150 for upgraded appointment with six guests. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

Just off Bryant Park is Bridal Reflections, a massive family-owned bridal salon. Those looking for the embellished styles of Kim Kassas, classic Pronovias silhouettes, and tons of selections from high-end designers can find them at this popular boutique.

Designers in Stock: Leah Da Gloria, Kim Kassas Couture, Adi Shlomo, Galia Lahav, Eve of Milady, Milla Nova, Enzoani, Lazaro, Maison Perez by Lazaro, Michael DePaulo, Pronovias, Maggie Sottero, Amalia Carrara by Eve of Milady, Shiran Abergel, Adam Zohar, Stephen Yearick, and Ysa Makino.

Appointment Fee: $100 for a standard appointment and $750 for a three-hour VIP appointment. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Does your style lean more eclectic? Then you’ll want to take a look at the selection of bridal looks at Belle Atelier. The salon offers dresses for those who want their wedding wardrobe to make a sartorial statement. In-house alterations are also a key part of the atelier’s ethos, and the salon even offers the ability to collaborate on custom designs.

Designers in Stock: Vivienne Westwood, Varca, Wed Studio, Bretagne, Di Petsa, Richard Quinn, and Prea James.

Appointment Fee: $25 for a mini appointment (1-2 dresses), $50 for a one-hour appointment, $120 for a two-hour appointment, and $35 for an accessories appointment.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Visiting Bergdorf Goodman is already a treat—but going to find your wedding dress is extra special. The department store carries a great selection of gowns and accessories from luxury bridal designers in its private bridal salon. Best of all, you can easily start on your shoe search afterwards a few floors below.

Designers in Stock: Andrew Kwon, Amsale, CD Greene, Cucculelli Shaheen, Elie Saab, Enaura, Giambattista Valli, Homa Bridal, Ines Di Santo, Jaclyn Whyte, Monvieve, Naeem Khan, Reem Acra, Sareh Nouri, The Danes New York, Vera Wang, Verdin Bridal, and Viktor & Rolf.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Although based in Brooklyn, The One Bridal is worth the subway ride. Some of our favorite designers from around the globe have this salon as their only stockist in the five boroughs. Come try on the designs, then spend the rest of your afternoon exploring Industry City.

Designers in Stock: Cortana, Flora, Halfpenny London, Lola Varma, Prea James, Sophie et Voilà, and The Law Bridal.

Appointment Fee: $40 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Danielle Frankel’s stunning new flagship in Tribeca cements the brand’s presence as the must-visit bridal destination in the city. Located in a converted Mercantile Exchange building, the multi-story salon is not only an aesthetic treat—interior designer Augusta Hoffman curated the space—but also houses Frankel’s fashion-forward gowns, accessories, and large fitting rooms for to-be-weds and their guests to try on garments.

Appointment Fee: $150 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

On the second floor of Oscar De La Renta’s Madison Avenue store, you’ll find the brand’s flagship bridal salon. From glamorous gowns to fun minis, brides can shop for their entire wedding wardrobe in this luxe space. Make sure to check out downstairs as well for colorful options for yourself and VIPs in your wedding party.

Alteration Services: The brand partners with outside alterations specialists.

Monique Lhuillier’s Upper East Side store is an essential stop on many brides-to-be’s shopping trips. Known for beautiful lace gowns and classic silhouettes, this bright and airy store offers a one-on-one styling session to help guide you towards your dream dress.

Appointment Fee: Complimentary. Appointment fee will be implemented in 2027.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

No name is as synonymous with bridal fashion as Vera Wang. If you want to try on the largest selection of the brand’s haute couture collections, head to its Upper East Side salon, where you can shop new collections and iconic styles from years past in the minimalist boutique.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Amsale has a light-filled flagship in SoHo that’s perfect for brides hoping to find a dress that fits a modern-meets-classic aesthetic. The salon offers a serene experience as you try your way through their refined silhouettes. The two-story boutique also has ready-to-wear styles perfect for guests, bridesmaids, and mothers of the bride and groom.

Dress Price Starting Point: $1995 for Nouvelle Amsale and $4000 for Amsale.

Appointment Fee: $50 hold fee that is refunded after appointment.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

The stylish interiors of Alexandra Grecco’s NYC flagship salon set the stage for a joyful shopping experience. The SoHo salon not only has the brand’s core silhouettes, but also a few flagship exclusives and runway accessories perfect for the bride looking to push the boundary with their wedding weekend style.

Appointment Fee: $125 for bridal appointment and $50 for accessories-only appointment. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

The moody interiors on Spring Street immediately draw you into the world of Cinq. The vintage-inspired gowns line the walls of this large showroom space, which offers individual appointments for brides to explore the salon with a dedicated stylist.

Appointment Fee: $150 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

If you want a truly original look for your wedding weekend, consider One/Of. Patricia Voto welcomes you into her jewel-box Upper East Side studio to craft a bespoke piece with original patterns, sourced designer and vintage deadstock fabric, and silhouettes chosen for your exact measurements. Understandably, this labor-intensive creative process raises the price tag, but it’s worth it for a fully custom piece.

Dress Price Starting Point: $16,000 for bespoke looks and $30,000 for bespoke wedding gowns

Appointment Fee: $500 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Wiederhoeft has become a favorite for couples seeking bold looks with intricate beading and artfully cinched waistlines. With the designer’s corsetry program that allows to-be-weds to perfectly fit their proportions based on bust and torso length, you can ensure the perfect fit as you head down the aisle or dance into the night. An appointment at the Garment District showroom starts with a corset fitting—and ends with you trying tons of fun runway looks.

Appointment Fee: $100 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

The New York flagship for Australian bridal brand Kyha is the bridal destination of NoHo. While clean, crafted silhouettes are the designer’s bread and butter, each season also brings about trend-forward styles for the bride looking to have some fun with their bridal style. Expect to celebrate with some Champagne as you shop your way through their selection.

Appointment Fee: $50 for accessories styling appointments, $60 for weekday appointments, and $100 for weekend appointments.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

If you love Galia Lahav’s signature lace gowns, the NYC flagship on Wooster Street is a must-visit. The bridal salon features a huge selection of the brand’s dresses from both their Galia and Couture lines, offering a wide range of styles to fit your aesthetic. Helpful stylists will guide you through the collections and offer treats for you and your party as you get laced into the designer’s many corseted styles.

Appointment Fee: $50 to $100 based on day of the week. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

NYC-based designer Sarah Seven has both her namesake line and luxury Sept collection housed in the same building on Lafayette Street. With specialized salons on separate floors, brides can book appointments to explore which styles might fit into their wedding wardrobes.

Dress Price Starting Point: $4,500 for Sarah Seven and $12,000 for Sept

Appointment Fee: $100 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

Milla Nova’s modern showroom is a new destination for brides-to-be downtown. The Ukrainian brand created a warm, minimal space to welcome clients to explore their collections and find their dream gown.

Appointment Fee: $60 for weekday appointments, $100 for weekend appointments, and $700 for private suite appointments. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Just off of Washington Square Park is Lee Petra Grebenau’s flagship salon. Here, you’ll find the designer’s beautiful lace gowns, fun embellished minis, and a select number of made-to-order styles perfect for reception looks. Stylists guide you through the selections, while providing insights into fit, customizations, and more.

Appointment Fee: $100 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

The bridal collections of Elie Saab are known for their meticulous construction and inventive takes on classic silhouettes. Luckily, the designer’s Madison Avenue store serves as a flagship for the bridal brand. To-be-weds can work with their experienced team to guide them through styling and alterations of their gorgeous gowns.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

With its beautiful corsetry and boundary-pushing aesthetics, Vivienne Westwood has become one of the most popular choices for stylish brides for a reason. The brand recently expanded the footprint of its bridal collection to take over the entire second floor of its NYC flagship, where to-be-weds can try a large selection of gowns from recent made-to-measure and couture collections.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

Anne Barge has transformed a chic Upper East Side apartment into their flagship store. With both their Blue Willow and Anne Barge lines available, as well as their shoe and accessory collections, brides can fully outfit themselves for the walk down the aisle.

Dress Price Starting Point: $2,850 for the Blue Willow collection and $3,700 for the Anne Barge collection

Appointment Fee: $50 for weekday appointments and $100 for weekend appointments. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Within the Garment District, you’ll find Enaura’s tastefully decorated bridal salon. Adjoining the brand’s atelier, the showroom allows you to have an individualized appointment with a stylist to try on a wide selection of looks from past seasons. Designer Sohil Mistry is also often on hand to discuss construction and speak to customizations.

Appointment Fee: $125 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: The brand partners with outside alterations specialists.

Lein is a NYC-based favorite to find polished pieces to fit every part of your wedding wardrobe journey. Designer Meredith Stoecklein’s SoHo showroom offers a personalized environment to engage with the brand and try styles from both the bridal and ready-to-wear collections. Lein also works on bespoke projects for clients looking to create something original.

Dress Price Starting Point: $1,500 for civil ceremony, $4000 for gowns, and bespoke pricing upon request.

Appointment Fee: $150 for standard appointments and $250 for bespoke. Fee is applied to purchases.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Brides who love a slinky slip or two-piece set should make an appointment at Elizabeth Fillmore’s Meatpacking District salon. Adjoining the designer’s HQ, the showroom allows to-be-weds to shop styles old and new from the chic collections.

Appointment Fee: $100 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

If you want to bring a vintage flair to your wedding attire without having to search for an archival piece, check out the collections of Tanner Fletcher. The brand has crafted a gender-inclusive bridal line that mixes beautiful technique with nostalgia and a sense of whimsy. While you can shop pieces that have made their way down the runways, the designers are always open to crafting custom creations for your big day.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

NYC-based brand Markarian has an intimate showroom in the Union Square neighborhood filled with its artfully designed pieces by recent Vogue bride Alexandra O’Neill. While you can find Markarian’s beautiful ready-to-wear styles in stock, the bridal pieces are worth visiting for on their own. If you’re looking to fill out your entire bridal wardrobe, Markarian has thoughtful pieces for more casual events as well as your walk down the aisle.

Appointment Fee: $150 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Salon recommends an outside alterations specialist.

Those drawn to Honor’s eclectic, feminine designs should pay a visit to the designer’s newly decorated SoHo salon. As the home base for the brand, you can find the largest selection of styles within these dusty pink interiors. Honor also offers bespoke experiences for brides looking for a special piece from creative director Giovanna Randall.

Appointment Fee: $215 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Andrew Kwon offers a white-glove shopping experience in the heart of NYC’s Garment District. Private showroom appointments allow you to be the only client in the room as you explore Kwon’s beautiful designs. If you’re interested in looks in shades other than white for yourself, a bridesmaid, or mother-of-the-bride, the designer’s evening collections are also on display in the showroom.

Appointment Fee: $150 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

When trying on wedding gowns, it’s important to be prepared so you can have the best overall experience. It’s advised to wear nude undergarments that won’t show through more sheer styles and consider bringing a heel you might like to wear with a gown. You should also avoid wearing heavy makeup and fragrances to appointments. Sample gowns are reworn by many to-be-weds, and many stores ask you to go fresh-faced to avoid makeup transfer. While you can bring a few guests along like a bridesmaid, mom, or stylist, check with each salon’s policies on how big of a party you can bring.

As most wedding dresses take six to eight months to make, it is advised to book your appointments about nine months to a year ahead of your wedding. On rare occasions, you can find designers who might be able to work on shorter timelines. Certain popular designers can book out their appointments months in advance, so as soon as you know you want to start the shopping process, take a look at availability.

#6607. Grand Theft Auto VI Welcomes a New Wave of (Virtual) Gym Bros

After a 13-year drought, Grand Theft Auto VI has finally hit the masses. Predictably, a large swath of guys have called off work to give themselves just enough time to explore the immersive fictional land of Leonida, where players can do just about everything they can in real life—from driving cars and renovating homes to playing video games within a video game. In Grand Theft Auto VI, that now also includes hitting the gym. And if you want to progress through the story as efficiently as possible, becoming an in-game gym rat might be the best thing you can do.

Expanding on a gameplay mechanic introduced in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, working out in GTA levels up your character to help with progressing through the story. The fitter you become in the game, the more stamina you have to sprint, the more health you have before you’re Wasted, and the more focus you have to take down enemies. Just like in real life, pumping iron makes daily life a whole lot easier.

To get fit, you can use the weights in Jason’s outdoor gym, which features the big three full-body lifts: squats, bench presses, and deadlifts. While your character handles the heavy lifting, all you have to do is carefully time your button presses to complete reps without causing an injury. Once you have enough money, you can purchase memberships at gyms across the city, giving you access to treadmills, free weights, and workout machines. The exercise options are so extensive (you can even do zone 2 cardio) that gamers have already started trading tips to the best GTA 6 workouts for maximizing your character’s gains.

As your character gets stronger, their avatar transforms accordingly, developing more defined muscles, a six-pack, and even a chiseled face. Neglecting your fitness and overeating (a real thing you can do in the game) has an alternate effect as your player visibly gains weight and adopts a “dad bod.”

Inevitably there will be many players that skip the gym this weekend so they can pump a little virtual iron with their thumbs. There’s something undeniably ironic about looksmaxxing your GTA character while spending hours sitting on the couch playing a video game. But don’t think that just because it’s all on a screen that you won’t walk away from a session with a little back pain, so maybe schedule a few breaks in between. You could even build a home gym of your own like Jason’s—it’s already got one fitness expert’s approval.

#6606. Who Is Miley Cyrus’s Husband, Maxx Morando?

The couple officially said “I do” in Palm Springs

Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando are officially married! Nearly one year after their engagement was confirmed, the couple tied the knot on Saturday, November 21, in Palm Springs, California.

The singer, who said “I do” in Saint Laurent, shared black-and-white photos from the wedding on Instagram, simply captioning the post, “M+M 🤍 11.21.26.” In photos, the couple could be seen exchanging vows in a poolside ceremony featuring a stunning display of sweeping white flowers and candles.

In December 2025, Cyrus confirmed her engagement to musician Maxx Morando—a relationship she has largely kept out of the spotlight following her highly publicized marriage to Liam Hemsworth. The Bass Persuades singer was first linked to Morando in November 2021, when the two sparked romance rumors with a joint appearance at the Gucci Love Parade fashion show. (Cyrus later shared a photo of herself with Morando from the event on Instagram.)

Rumors escalated the following month, when Cyrus danced and held hands with Morando in Miami during her New Year’s Eve Party special for NBC. By April 2022, they confirmed their romance during an outing in West Hollywood, where they went all out with the PDA.

Fast forward to the 2024 Grammys and Morando supported Cyrus at the show—where she won her first Grammy for “Flowers”—and he gave her a passionate kiss.

Since then, the two have kept their relationship low-key aside from a few red carpet appearances together. But while Morando has mostly kept his personal life out of the public spotlight, he, like Cyrus, has had a long career in music.

Ahead, everything we know about Cyrus’s new husband, Maxx Morando.

While best known as the drummer for Liily (and for the Regrettes, from 2015 to 2018), Morando also plays guitar. Additionally, he has also collaborated with Cyrus on several of her albums, including her most recent release, Bass Persuades. For the project, he co-produced the album’s title track alongside Cyrus, as well as several others, including “Aftermath” and “REDLIGHTS.” The musician also has songwriting credits, co-writing “Innocent Ways” with Cyrus and being credited on “Aftermath.”

Morando also produced two songs, “Handstand” and “Violet Chemistry,” from the singer’s Endless Summer Vacation LP.

He also collaborated with Cyrus on her 2025 album, Something Beautiful, contributing as both a producer and songwriter on several tracks. Morando also played drums on the record and made a cameo in the “End of the World” music video.

The drummer, born in 1998, is six years Cyrus’s junior. (His birthday also happens to fall exactly a week ahead of the singer’s, on November 16.)

Cyrus opened up about their slight age gap in a 2024 interview with Harper’s Bazaar: “He grew up with a laptop. I had a desktop computer that I shared with my brothers and sisters. … Honestly, he’s raised our dog off Reddit. I’m like, Are you sure we’re supposed to be doing this? And he’s like, On Reddit it says blah, blah, blah.”

Along with his musical endeavors, the drummer has dabbled in fashion design too, with Cyrus as his muse.

Cyrus revealed in September 2021 that Morando contributed cartoon designs to a custom vegan leather set by designer Shane Kastl, which Cyrus wore for a performance that month.

“This look is a one-of-a-kind collaboration between two of my favorite emerging artists, Maxx Morando and Shane Kastl,” Cyrus said of the special look in an interview. “Their collaboration is the perfect example of sustainability becoming the next fashion phase, and it proves that anything can be reinvented, which resonates with me deeply.”

In an interview for Bazaar’s December 2024 cover story, Cyrus opened up about her relationship with Morando, saying, “He’s very similar to me. We just don’t take life too seriously.”

She also shared how working with Morando on musical projects helped them bond: “I worked with my dad forever. That’s how me and my ex-husband met each other. I’ve always worked with the people that I love,” Cyrus says. “And Maxx just inspires me so much.”

The couple’s engagement was confirmed in December 2025, after Cyrus sparked rumors by wearing a diamond sparkler on her left-hand ring finger at the premiere of Avatar: Fire and Ash in LA.

Morando keeps an extremely private, low profile in both his personal and professional life. While the musician does have an Instagram, he rarely posts, aside from sharing new music that he works on with both his band and Cyrus.

In March 2023, a source told People that Morando is a “cool guy” who is drama-free, a trait that Cyrus finds extremely attractive.

“He has no interest in being a huge celebrity; he’s very low-key. Miley loves these qualities,” the source said. “Miley can be herself. They are supportive of each other’s careers. Miley is enjoying life and things are great.”

Following a year-long engagement, the Morando and Cyrus officially wed in an intimate ceremony held in Palm Springs, California. The couple shared photos from the wedding on Instagram, which included black-and-white portraits of the couple with their dog, as well as a sweet photo of them kissing after saying “I do.”

For the ceremony, the bride wore a long-sleeve, backless Saint Laurent wedding gown, while Morando kept things classic in a black suit.

The poolside ceremony took place at Frank Sinatra’s former home, which was transformed with hundreds of white roses for the occasion. In photos obtained by DeuxMoi, the couple could be seen exchanging vows by the pool, in front of an intimate crowd of guests dressed in all-black attire.

#6605. Shop the Best Hoop Earrings—No Jewelry Box Is Complete Without a Pair

*All products featured on *Vogue are independently selected by our editors. However, we may earn affiliate revenue on this article and commission when you buy something

Few jewelry pieces have quite the staying power of a good hoop earring. It’s one of the most essential pieces in one’s jewelry collection, complements almost any outfit, and never goes out of style. Whether you prefer gold, silver, huggies or jumbo hoops, this classic go-to style holds the power to pull together any look. Its appeal lies in the versatility—there’s an appropriate version for every occasion. Pair a simple gold Jennifer Fisher Samira hoop with a white button-down and jeans to polish off your everyday uniform, or add sparkly pavés to your evening look to make a statement.

Jewelry designer Jennifer Fisher, hoop aficionado, has said it’s the one jewelry piece her clients rely on most when wanting to feel more polished. Fisher would concur–there’s no denying the power of a good accessory. She’s played a part in accessorizing some of society’s most influential, from Jennifer Lopez to former first lady Michelle Obama in her coveted hoop earrings. Who better to discuss building a hoop earring collection with than the Queen of Hoops herself?

Fisher recommends starting with small hoop earrings. “Your first pair should be something clean that you can wear morning, noon, and night.” From there, perhaps you gradually add some flair. “Your fifth pair of hoops should be something that has texture and maybe a larger diameter. Something that rounds out your collection.”

According to Fisher, hoop earrings are the blue jeans of the jewelry world–timeless, comfortable, and a wardrobe piece everyone should own. “I always say that hoop earrings are like the perfect pair of jeans–you need a few styles to round out your collection,” Fisher continues. “Your foundation is normally something pretty classic, and then as you grow your collection, your selection should become more diverse. A great example: For your first pair of jeans, you probably aren’t going to buy a wide-leg, long version. You’re probably going to go with a classic straight-leg version, so I suggest the same idea when you’re buying hoops.” Following those building blocks, start with a classic 18k gold huggie as the foundation. Then maybe you branch out to a medium size, perhaps go chunky, try some two-tone mixed metals, or consider a drop earring with gemstones…the list goes on.

No jewelry collection is complete without at least one (or two…or three) gold hoop earrings. Whether you’re building your personal edit from the ground up, contemplating a jewelry gift to self, or simply looking for a few new variations to add to your jewelry box, below is Vogue’s guide to the best hoop earrings on the market.

Huggies are the tiny versions of hoop earrings that sit really close to the earlobe, wrapping around just like a hug (hence the name). In 14K yellow gold, huggie hoop earrings are the perfect low-effort, never-take-off pieces you can shower, swim, and sleep in without much notice or care. They’re also great if you, like myself, love to layer. Add them to your second, third, or fourth hole, or all of the above for a really cool look.

These are the in-between styles that are a bit larger than the huggie hoop style we just discussed, but smaller than the oversized stunner pieces we’ll touch on later. Go for a solid gold everyday hoop or choose something more elaborate—we love the intricate fine jewelry creations from Lucy Delius and Tabayer.

An oversized hoop earring is a classic statement piece and can really add drama to your look. Those with sensitive ear though may want to opt for a thinner pair like these Anita Ko diamond hoop earrings rather than something chunky. If you’re anything like me and want to make a statement, try this silver-plated Rachel Comey pair.

Jewelry is often referred to as art. Some of the most fun hoops aren’t just a circle in a piercing–but perhaps include a twist, a turn, or a spiral that loops around the ear in suspend motion. This sparkly Swarovski pair are amazing for a night out; for everyday wear, we love Charlotte Chesnais’s architectural silver hoop earrings, which curve gracefully the lobe.

A little color goes a long way. Whether it’s a fun mustard yellow leather like this So-Le Studio hoop, or a vibrant emerald-adorned Anita Ko pair, you can comfortably skip a necklace when you’re rocking a statement hoop.

#6603. How the Holy Is Revered and Corrupted in The Body

Netflix’s buzzy new show, created by Quinn Shephard, examines guilt, God, and control through the eyes of teen girls attending a Catholic high school

I wanted nothing more than to see the Holy Spirit. One day after church, my grandfather described the moment he first believed was witnessing the Holy Spirit: a soothing, cleansing sensation in which God, in some way, possessed and reassured your mind. Divine intervention felt attainable for a moment. At first, I, too, hoped to discover serenity, an especially enticing thought since my parents were far less religious. But over time, that belief twisted in my preteen mind, instilling instead a fear that every misstep might damn me. To be viewed unfavorably by God—as a kid—is a terrifying thought. And it lingers.

I soon let go of the institutionalized beliefs. Yet, a longing to believe in something greater—especially when facing the unknown—never fully left me. I still desired to find spiritual ground, one free from this all-consuming, stress-fueling shame. This friction between spiritual surrender and self-actualization is the beating heart of Quinn Shephard’s The Body. Beneath a relentless downpour of religious guilt and an insatiable appetite for forgiveness, the students at St. Mark’s Catholic High School battle their inner demons as they discern what they want for themselves versus what the world expects of them.

Shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell thrust the audience into an age of Razor flip phones, AOL instant messaging, and Juicy Couture tracksuits, all set to a 2000s soundtrack featuring Kylie Minogue and No Doubt. Its barbed-edged storytelling draws comparisons to Cruel Intentions and Pretty Little Liars, with a bewitching touch of Jennifer’s Body or The Crucible. Here, girl teenagedom traverses suppressed sapphic love and the systemic weaponization of religious guilt—an incisive critique biting enough to solicit a petition with over 120,000 people pushing to cancel it. This coming-of-age series emerges from the dual nature of what we hold sacred: its capacity for reverence and its vulnerability to corruption.

Catholic school scares me. Teenagers scare me more, especially Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), the hyper-religious, manipulative student at the heart of the story. At first, The Body introduces us to Lisbeth as the quintessential “weird kid,” socially ostracized because of her eyebrow-less face and her freakishly religious family. (She evokes Carrie in Carrie.) But as The Body unfolds, Lisbeth pulls—or rather, tugs—at the web of guilt ensnaring the school’s dance team, the Lions, concerning the near-death of their new teammate, Grace (Sofia Wylie). Grace fell into a coma shortly after the girls pretended to sacrifice her at a Halloween party, popping ecstasy pills they referred to as the “body of Satan.” This hazing ritual is all in good fun until Grace’s heart actually stops … if only briefly.

The aftermath casts a shadow of guilt over everything—especially for Anya (Kristina Bogic), queen bee and dance team captain, who moved Grace’s unconscious body back to her bedroom with Lisbeth’s help. Soon after, Anya begins to see visions of Grace in her dreams. The moment she confesses this to the group, the other girls start confirming visions of their comatose friend. This uncanny groupthink preys on the girls with something to hide, who carry shame with them wherever they go. Anya, for instance, feels deep contrition for her romantic feelings for her best friend Elise (Sarah Boustany), whereas Elise more boldly embraces her queer sexuality. Elise faces the world with a steady confidence, shielding her from spiritual panic—and its subsequent manipulation.

The same isn’t true for most of her teammates, all of whom seek solace in the intangible, in God and the Holy Spirit, in the saintly visions of Grace. Grace then becomes a symbol of the sacred, a story that inspires people and therefore can be corrupted to control others. The girls’ desperate need for forgiveness makes them vulnerable to Lisbeth’s manipulation. When the team goes on a getaway together, they take hallucinogenic mushrooms before deciding that they must purge evil spirits from Grace by way of an exorcism (led by Lisbeth, of course). Lisbeth controls this ritual, forcing each girl to confess their sins. (She already knows them all after reading all their private messages.) Her feigned omniscience incites hysteria among the girls.

Shame clouds nearly all the girls’ minds. Maddie (Shirley Chen) wrestles with an eating disorder, some girls admit to premarital sex or impure thoughts, and Lisbeth attempts to squeeze out a confession from Elise about her feelings for Anya. The Body runs the gamut of teenage girlhood, but Shephard distills these insecurities into a single critique of control: how the holy—the fear of God—can exploit people, corrupt what we see, and shape what we believe. In episode 6, “Star Quality,” mass hysteria breaks out in the town, with people associated with the church now believing to see visions and revere Grace as a saintly figure. It’s driven by an innate desire to be seen—to see something—and a desperate desire to be part of something larger.

This same desire, to witness something collectively transcendent, forged the foundation of my spiritual beliefs. It also scared me enough to run from them. A connection to God came with fear of hellfire and the shame of sin. In this way, forgiveness felt like something I received out of desperation, rather than salvation. The Body studies the dangers of this unmitigated belief, of a doctrine designed to parse out the unknown. But by whose authority? Shephard’s story reminds us that the storyteller—the pastor or the manipulative teenage girl—controls the things we see and the things we may believe.

#6602. Author Josh Silver’s Brooch Game? It’s Strong

Author Josh Silver has been having quite the whirlwind year—thanks to his debut adult novel, Fruit Fly, which was released in August and is now a New York Times bestseller. Don’t call the book’s plot meta, though it does draw loose parallels to Silver’s own budding literary life: The dark satirical thriller follows a struggling author who “exploits a vulnerable young man’s life” to write his novel. “The whole thing has felt completely surreal, honestly,” Silver tells Vogue of releasing his buzzy breakout work. “Getting to travel and watch a story that started in my own head connect with readers all over the world is a feeling I don't think I’ll ever quite get used to.”

Last week, Silver continued his months-long press tour for the book—this time, by attending the National Book Awards in New York City as a special guest. “It was an amazing way to cap off a busy year—getting to be in one room with so many of my personal heroes,” says Silver, who appreciated the opportunity to celebrate the art of writing. “Especially right now, it feels vital to celebrate the people fighting to keep diverse stories and voices on the shelves.” The cherry on top, meanwhile? He attended the event wearing a sleek and snazzy Celine tuxedo by Michael Rider.

Styled by Christopher Rao, Silver’s polished look consisted of a black wool-and-mohair Celine tuxedo finished off with a white poplin dress shirt, black silk tie, leather belt, and lambskin jazz shoes. (Dance shoes are in, as you know.) “The tailoring is just razor-sharp,” says Silver of his smart, modern look. “It feels classic, and effortlessly cool all at once.”

Even more special were the thematic brooches that he punctuated the ensemble with. “My stylist Christopher paired it with these incredible 1940s Van Cleef & Arpels diamond fly brooches from FD Gallery,” Silver says. “They’re a little nod to the book, and honestly, I feel very lucky to be wearing them. The whole look is really smart.” He also wore earrings and rings from Prounis Jewelry.

You could say the dapper formal attire served as an extremely amped-up version of the author’s everyday style: He certainly isn’t rocking priceless jewels and bespoke tailoring while writing away at his desk every day. “Day-to-day, I’m quite low-key—mostly living in comfortable basics while I’m at my laptop,” he says. (What? Did you expect him to write in couture?) “That’s why nights like [the Book Awards] are so fun—I don’t get to clean up like this very often,” he says.

Through the end of the year, meanwhile, you’ll find Silver slipping back into his basics, toiling away at home: Fans will be pleased to know he’s working on his next highly-anticipated book. “It’s coming along nicely,” he teases, without giving anything away. “After all the travel this year, I’m actually really excited to just put my head down, disappear into that world, and finish it.” As are we.

#6601. The Las Vegas Grand Prix Kicks Off With a Disco Bash by SkinCeuticals

Outside, the city of Las Vegas is readying its streets for this weekend’s Formula One Grand Prix, when the world’s fastest drivers in the world’s fastest cars will tear down the Strip at 200-plus miles per hour. But inside Sin City’s hot spots, the starry F1 events are just getting started—and everyone at the SkinCeuticals Las Vegas Grand Prix Party quite literally had their (glowing) game faces on.

On Wednesday night, SkinCeuticals, as the official skincare partner of Scuderia Ferrari HP, hosted an exclusive bash at Baby Disco, the intimate, moody lounge tucked away within Zero Bond at The Wynn Las Vegas.

With the space aglow in Ferrari Rosso Scuderia red under a shiny mirrored disco ball and a checkered-flag DJ booth, guests snacked on wagyu bites and gourmet caviar-topped chicken nuggets and sipped on-theme cocktails. (Also served: SkinCeuticals’s top-shelf favorites, including the P-TIOX and C E Ferulic serums, passed around on silver trays.) The model Kelly Piquet, partner of F1 star Max Verstappen, posted up on the green velvet banquette, as other attendees played around with SkinCeuticals-branded poker chips and cards around the room.

On the venue’s outdoor terrace overlooking the glowing marvel that is Sphere, actor Chace Crawford and his dad, dermatologist Chris Wayne Crawford, took a moment to enjoy the view. The two were doing a little father-son bonding—a perfect setting since F1 is “a male, testosterone-fueled sport,” joked Chris. As a Texas native, Chace (who also came through GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party in LA last week) has seen the F1 Grand Prix in Austin, but he’s excited to catch his first race under the megawatt Vegas lights. “It’s surreal out here,” said the The Boys star, looking out over the Strip.

Inside, sportscaster and former Seattle Seahawk superstar Russell Wilson, a big F1 fan, couldn’t wait for lights-out-and-away-we-go on Sunday. He’s attended F1 races in Monaco and Montreal, but he really digs the Vegas experience. “I’m racing around the track tomorrow night,” he said, “so I’m fired up about it.”

At 9 p.m. the party kicked into high gear as Alex Pall and Drew Taggart of the Chainsmokers took to the DJ booth, easing into their set, kicking off a remix of thesynth-pop classic “Don't You Want Me” then incrementally dialing up the heat until Taggart took to the mic himself to perform “Paris,” the DJ duo’s 2017 hit. When the musician Sooin, of the K-pop group Meovv, hopped into the booth to chop it up with the Chainsmokers, the room lit up.

They closed out their set with some on-theme bottle service, as the Baby Disco crew made their way through the crowd hoisting magnums of Champagne and a strobe-flashing disco ball shaped like SkinCeuticals’s iconic serum dropper bottle. Time for the cooldown lap.

“I just want to say, everyone has really nice skin in here,” Taggart told the room with a grin. “Shout out to SkinCeuticals.”

#6599. Who Is Miley Cyrus’s New Husband, Maxx Morando?

Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando have kept things pretty low-key across their five-year relationship—so low-key, in fact, that their sporadic public appearances tend to be followed by questions on social media like, “Who’s Miley’s hot date?” Well, it’s Maxx Morando, drummer for the Los Angeles rock band Liily—and now, Cyrus’s husband.

Below, find everything you need to know about Maxx Morando, a.k.a. the new Mr. Miley Cyrus, whom Cyrus married in a poolside ceremony over the weekend in Palm Springs.

Cyrus and Morando met on a blind date in 2021. (“Well, it was blind for me and not really for him,” Cyrus told British Vogue in 2023.) They’ve been living together in Malibu since at least 2024.

Morando and Cyrus at the Guicci Love Parade show in Los Angeles in November 2021.

Before joining Liily, Morando played drums for indie rock band the Regrettes from 2015 to 2018.

Cyrus invited Morando and Liily to perform on her New Year’s Eve special on NBC in 2022, with a source saying at the time: “Miley insisted that Maxx’s band perform at her NYE special, and this was not something up for debate. Music is what bonds them together and they love nothing more than creating beautiful sounds when it is just the two of them.” Additionally, Morando and Cyrus worked together on the songs “Handstand” and “Violet Chemistry” from her 2023 album Endless Summer Vacation; and he contributed to several songs on this year’s Bass Persuades.

If you were Miley Cyrus, wouldn’t you ditch your phone occasionally? Apparently, that’s exactly what the star does, telling British Vogue of the couple’s phone protocol: “My boyfriend brings his phone and I don’t bring one.” If he’s willing to be plugged into the extremely online world for you, he might just be a keeper.

Cyrus and Morando had discussed getting engaged prior to a 2025 trip to Japan, but he finally pulled off a surprise proposal in what he described as “this beautiful Japanese forest-y situation” on their hotel grounds. “I could feel my heart pounding. You grow up as a kid watching the movies where the guy gets on one knee and does the whole thing, and you know that’s what you’re supposed to do. But then you realize, ‘Okay, I literally have to get on one knee.’ I didn’t want to fuck up and fumble or drop the [ring].” Well, it seems he didn’t (or if he did, Cyrus presumably found it endearing)!

#6598. 14 Best Barn Coats for Men in 2026, According to GQ Editors

The best barn coats for men are a close cousin of the chore jacket—similar in spirit, but built tougher. They’re heartier, heavier, better insulated, and usually more water-resistant. Where the chore jacket belonged to the factory floor, the barn coat was made for the fields: a layer you could shrug on to tackle chores outdoors.

But ever since the ’80s and ’90s, the barn coat has been finding a new audience of urbanites who understand its utility, even on mean city streets. Today, alongside the waxy Barbour zip-ups and dad-approved L.L. Bean riffs, a ton of capital-F fashion labels—The Row, Auralee, Prada—have been herding the barn coat back into the center of the style conversation.

Reading to buy your first barn coat? Make sure it’s cut with enough room to comfortably slip a sweater beneath it, and that its craftsmanship ensures it’ll remain a reliable rotation beater for years to come. The former, of course, might demand some trial and error on your end, but the latter is exactly where we come in. These are the absolute best barn coats for men on the market right now, from the genre-defining joints you already know to the sleeper-hit versions you probably don’t.

Deep, easily accessed pockets? A warm corduroy collar? A charming plaid lining? This jacket from J.Crew is, quite simply, the platonic ideal of a barn coat. It has all the details dialed in, built upon a sturdy, 100% cotton washed canvas body that will only soften and feel more like your own in time. Originally launched over 40 years ago, there’s a reason J.Crew is still able to sell it four decades later. And we didn’t even mention the hook on the back, so you can hang this up with ease as soon as you enter your bustling, warm, overcrowded local bar. It’s the little things.

I should disclose up front that I’m a bit of an OrSlow obsessive. I own more from the brand than I’ll ever admit publicly or privately and doubt that I’ve ever been unaware of something it’s produced, but this is because no brand has more consistently lived-up to pre-purchase expectations in my illustrious shopping career, and the only things that see the light of day are things that are absolutely dialed. And this jacket is dialed, folks. Made in Japan from start to finish, it has the kind of cut that can handle a Joey Tribbiani-esque volume of layers, is made from a cotton canvas fabric that will look unreal in half a decade, and the type of construction that other brands show factories when they’re trying to describe what they’re looking for.

We couldn’t round out a piece on barn coats without a nod to L.L. Bean, one of the OGs of the style. A century ago, Bean launched a rugged duck-hunting coat that slowly shifted into a catch-all field jacket—the ancestor of the one they’re still selling today. It’s made from hefty, water-resistant canvas, with a sewn-in lining, five roomy pockets, underarm gussets, and bi-swing shoulders so you can actually move in it. And like many things Bean, the sizing is inclusive, there’s even a “Tall” option for the vertically gifted among us.

The Real McCoy’s is known for painstakingly recreating vintage garments—the Abercrombie set that Hunter S. Thompson made famous is an all-timer—so you can bank on the fact that this barn jacket has all the proper credentials. If you are dubious, however, know that it’s made out of a damn-near-bulletproof cotton canvas fabric, is fully lined with twill to trap some heat when things get chilly, has a perfect hit of corduroy at the collar and comes equipped with one of the sickest pocket configurations you’ll ever see in the genre. It’s hard to call anything “perfect,” but I feel comfortable saying that this is an ideal barn jacket, and would be hard to beat against any rubric.

What’s all this, then—a Barbour as a barn coat? The Beaufort isn’t cut from the same stiff American canvas, but the brief is identical: a country jacket for tramping through fields, feeding the chickens, or—let’s be honest—making it to the pub. King Charles even reinstated the brand’s Royal Warrant last year (he is the Menswear King, after all). Built long before DWR and Gore-Tex, its waxed cotton shrugs off rain, the oversize corduroy collar blocks the wind, and you can zip in liners or snap on a hood if you feel like accessorizing. Best detail? The little hand-warmer pockets perched above the main ones—perfect for thawing fingers after a day of grouse shooting or a lap of the Lower East Side. Just remember: it will need the occasional re-waxing, but that’s all part of the fun.

If you're getting hung up on the idea of a barn jacket that’s implicitly unqualified to do barn jacket work, this isn’t going to be the one for you. But you if think that the barn jacket can be both a highly-functional, historically-revered workwear staple AND that it’s a brilliant canvas on which the most tasteful among us can mess around a little, this one from the maniacs (complimentary) at Auralee is hypnotic. The outer is made from a cotton moleskin—which is like flannel’s heavyweight cousin, for those unfamiliar—that’s been unevenly garment-dyed to look like it’s endured thousands of miles on a tractor. Meanwhile, the pockets are flawless, the zipped placket comes outfitted with a buttoned storm flap, and the whole thing is garnished with a detachable shearling collar, just in case you thought they spared a single expense along the way.

Knickerbocker is known for tasteful pieces that can help you rebuild an entire wardrobe, and that includes this faithful homage to vintage fly-fishing wading jackets commonly worn in the jacket’s namesake upstate region. The Portuguese canvas and rounded collar stand out among other jackets on our list, and the gusseted shoulders allow for a wide range of movement on and off the river.

First off, don't fear the red colorway. It's just as easy to wear as any other fall-adjacent color and it stands out roughly twice as much, which is kind of the dream ratio for eye-catching jackets. Also, it's just a damn-good barn coat, with deep ol' hand pockets, a wind-stopping corduroy collar and endless layering potential.

This is absolutely a barn jacket. All the hallmarks are there, from the corduroy collar (more on that later) to the generous pocket situation and layout. But it's also one of the most stunning corduroy jackets on the market due to one of the most breathtaking corduroys you will ever see. And if you ever were wondering, why don't they make the whole jacket out of the collar, they do.

Filson's classic Barn-adjacent coat is an undeniable giant in the space—big ol' stow pockets, corduroy collar, canvas outer—but the insulated iteration is every bit as easy to wear and twice as warm, without adding much bulk at all.

Think of this TS joint as the ultimate "what if." Like, what if, instead of a classic canvas outer there was a super soft, ultra sturdy, almost flannel-like flocked denim? And instead of corduroy, TS threw in a leather collar? Because across the board, they decided to find out.

Much like the Auralee number up top, this isn't the kind of barn jacket that you'd be wearing to bale hay, but there's only a select few among us doing that anyways. You can, however, wear the living hell out of this all winter long, because not only does it layer beautifully, it has the requisite storage, showstopping potential and only gets better with age. Is it practical? That's not the point.

Levi’s takes a no-nonsense swing at the barn jacket—exactly what you’d expect from them. You get a sturdy shell, a quilted lining that brings just the right amount of warmth, and two generous front pockets. Sure, it skips the classic hand-warmer pockets, but at a price this good, you can afford to overlook a detail or two.

This is one of the most affordable options on this list, but you're not leaving a ton on the table if this is your prefered route. The outer is a waxed organic cotton that will hold up well against all forms of precipitation, there's a full flannel lining and the collar even buttons into a stand, to really keep things insulated.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6597. Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando Are Married! See All the Photos Here

On Saturday, November 21, Miley Cyrus married Maxx Morando—poolside in Palm Springs, with the ceremony officiated by the Flaming Lips’ Wayne Coyne. Congratulations to the very happy rock stars!

33-year-old Cyrus and Morando, 28, tied the knot in front of an intimate crowd of family and friends, underneath a dramatic archway framed by white florals and candles. (Because when you can buy yourself flowers, why not buy out all of Hollywood’s florists for your nuptials?)

The bride chose Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello (does this make Cyrus Vaccarello’s last bridal moment for the house?), wearing a long-sleeved silk gown with matching silk slingback pumps. Her jewelry was Chopard: Cyrus chose 18k white gold set earrings with 4.27 carats of diamonds, along with a white gold set and diamond ring. As photographed by noted bridal photographer Jose Villa, Morando, too, wore Saint Laurent, pairing a single-breasted tuxedo jacket and trousers in grain de poudre with a crisp cotton poplin shirt, silk satin tie, SL 970 sunglasses, and grained leather Lewis sneakers. While her blonde hair was in a chicly loose and twisted up-do with height at the crown, Morando’s was his classic tousled and layered mullet.

In other photos obtained by People, Cyrus can be seen smiling brightly and wiping away tears as Morando shared his vows. Onlookers were dressed in all-black black-tie looks.

Cyrus’s mother Tish Cyrus and her partner Dominic Purcell, father Billy Ray and his partner Elizabeth Hurley, and her sister Noah were all in attendance. It was reported that the couple held their rehearsal the previous day.

On Monday—also Cyrus’s 34th birthday—the couple shared a new batch of images, showcasing the entirety of the day from the getting-ready process to the post-ceremony festivities. Alongside shots of the couple sharing their vows surrounded by palm trees, Cyrus also shared a photo of her Saint Laurent slingbacks laid alongside a monogrammed “M&M 11.21.26” handkerchief, as well as a snap of herself wiping away happy tears at the altar. (Also in the mix were images of Cyrus being walked down the aisle by her mom, and dancing with her dad at the reception.)

Then, there were a series of photos documenting the after-party, for which Cyrus changed into a black sequined minidress paired with sheer black tights and heels. Those heels were swiftly discarded, however, for dancing on chairs—before the happy couple made a classic getaway in the backseat of a vintage Mercedes.

Cyrus and Morando have been together for five years and were engaged in 2025. The bride previously confirmed that they first met on a blind date. “Well, it was blind for me and not really for him,” she told British Vogue. “I thought, ‘The worst that can happen is I leave.’” The pair went red carpet official at Gucci’s “Love Parade” show in November 2021.

Morando proposed to the “Flowers” singer during a vacation in Japan to celebrate her 33rd birthday. “I am not easy to surprise,” she admitted on Good Morning America following the news of her engagement. “I love to control every situation. I had completely surrendered. I’m telling you, I was so, so, so surprised.”

Her engagement ring is a cushion-cut stone on a thick, 14k yellow gold band by designer Jacquie Aiche, which the designer made bespoke for the couple: vintage-inspired, romantic, and elegant.

Morando is a drummer for the rock band Liily (who played at Cyrus’s 2022 New Year’s Eve special on NBC), as well as a songwriter and producer. The two have collaborated on multiple projects, including Cyrus’s 2023 album Endless Summer Vacation and her 2025 visual album Something Beautiful. Last month, the couple sang a duet of Cyrus’s “Let’s Get Married” on the Hollywood Bowl stage.

“I’ve always worked with the people that I love. And Maxx just inspires me so much,” Cyrus told Harper’s Bazaar of their creative work together. She added, “He’s very similar to me. We just don’t take life too seriously.”

Congratulations once again to Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando!
